ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,A complaint is an informal concern about service quality — the nurse was late. the visit was too short. You address what you can. document it. and submit it to your supervisor. A grievance is a formal allegation that patient rights were violated. It requires a documented intake. administrative review. and a written response within ten working days. An allegation is suspected abuse. neglect. or exploitation. It requires immediate mandatory reporting under state law. Suspicion is sufficient. You do not need proof.,A split-screen comparison showing three types of events with different severity icons. ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,Protected Health Information is any information that can identify a patient and relates to their health status. care. or payment. There are eighteen categories of PHI — name. address. date of birth. phone number. photos. and twelve others. A HIPAA violation does not require intent. ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,The minimum necessary standard means you use or disclose only the PHI needed to accomplish the specific task — nothing more. You are permitted to share PHI for three purposes without patient authorization: treatment with the direct care team. payment and billing. and healthcare operations such as quality review. You may not share PHI with an employer. with a family member who does not have authorization. or with anyone not directly involved in the patient's care.,A secure medical record icon surrounded by a shield with three labeled access zones: Treatment, Payment, Operations. Clean vector illustration style.,A 45-second animated card. Three green permission doors open — Treatment, Payment, Operations. Your phone. your tablet. your work laptop. even the paperwork on your front seat. The field environment creates security risks that a clinical facility doesn't have — you work in patient homes. in your car. in public spaces. Use only agency-approved apps to access the EHR. Lock your car whenever patient documents are inside. Never photograph a patient without documented consent. Prohibited: texting PHI over personal SMS. Posting anything patient-related on social media. Accessing patient records over unsecured public Wi-Fi. The right to amend inaccurate information. The right to an accounting of disclosures. And the right to request restrictions on use. ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,A breach is any unauthorized access. use. or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its security or privacy. When you discover or suspect a breach. report to your Privacy Officer immediately — do not wait until your shift ends. do not wait for confirmation that harm occurred. The agency has sixty days to notify affected patients and Health and Human Services. Your immediate report is what starts that process.,A nurse on the phone reporting a concern to a supervisor with a serious and professional expression. Indoor setting. Natural light. ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,Standard precautions exist for one reason: you cannot tell who is infectious by looking at them. Many patients with bloodborne infections have no symptoms. A patient who looks and feels healthy can transmit HBV. HCV. or HIV through a single exposure. Standard precautions are not applied to high-risk patients — they are applied to all patients. all the time.,A home health nurse donning gloves before entering a patient's home. Clean, professional. Natural daylight. Photorealistic. Confident and safe demeanor.,A 30-second animated card. Patient silhouettes all labeled with a question mark. Standard precautions shield covers all of them equally. Text: Every patient. Every visit.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,Standard precautions apply to blood. all body fluids except sweat. non-intact skin. and mucous membranes. The five moments of hand hygiene are: before touching the patient. before any aseptic procedure. after body fluid exposure risk. after touching the patient. and after touching patient surroundings. Soap and water for fifteen to twenty seconds. Alcohol-based hand rub for twenty to thirty seconds. Important: alcohol-based hand rub does not kill C. diff or norovirus. Use soap and water for those.,A nurse performing the five-moment hand hygiene process at a patient's kitchen sink. Step-by-step visual. Photorealistic. Clear and educational.,A 45-second animated five-moment sequence. Each moment appears with an icon and label. Timer shows 15-20 seconds for soap and water. Red alert icon for C. diff and norovirus: Use soap and water.,45 seconds

ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,PPE selection must match the procedure's exposure risk. Wearing gloves for a blood draw is not enough if splatter is possible — you also need eye protection. Bag technique is your infection barrier between patients. If your bag touches a contaminated surface and then opens at your next patient's home. you have transferred that contamination.,A nurse opening her nursing bag on a disposable blue pad on a patient's kitchen table. Gloves on. Professional and deliberate. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. PPE icons match to procedure risk level. Bag technique diagram shows barrier placement on a surface.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,PPE matrix: gloves for any body fluid contact. Gown when fluid splash or environmental contamination is likely. Surgical mask for droplet precautions. N95 for airborne precautions. Eye protection for any splash risk during a procedure. Bag technique: place your bag on a disposable barrier — never on the floor. never on the kitchen counter without a barrier. Clean your hands before and after accessing the bag. Keep it closed when you are not actively retrieving supplies.,A nursing bag on a clean disposable barrier on a table next to a gloved nurse's hands. Professional infection control setup. Photorealistic.,A 45-second PPE matrix animation. Five procedure types each get the correct PPE icon highlighted. Then bag technique steps shown as clean numbered animation.,45 seconds

What do you document?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV is most effective when started within two hours of exposure. After seventy-two hours it loses its effectiveness entirely. Every minute between exposure and medical evaluation is part of the therapeutic window. The post-exposure response protocol is not a suggestion — it is a timed medical response.,A nurse washing her hands at a sink with urgency. Clock visible on the wall showing the current time. Photorealistic. Clean clinical feeling in a home setting.,A 30-second animated clock countdown card. HIV PEP effectiveness bar decreases after 2 hours and reaches zero at 72 hours. Bold text: Every minute counts.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,After a needlestick: one. remove your glove and wash the site with soap and water for at least thirty seconds. Two. call your supervisor immediately — not tomorrow. within two hours. Three. seek medical evaluation at the designated facility within two hours. This is where the PEP decision is made. Four. document source patient information to facilitate bloodborne pathogen testing if the patient consents. Five. complete the exposure incident report before you leave for the day.,A nurse at a sink washing her hands with soap and water with a focused expression. A phone is visible on the counter showing she will be calling next. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated 5-step protocol. Each step appears numbered with a time requirement label. Step 3 flashes with a 2-hour urgency indicator.,45 seconds

ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,Communication barriers are not exceptions in home health. They are the rule. The average home health patient is elderly. managing multiple conditions. receiving complex medication instructions. and may have language. hearing. cognitive. or emotional barriers that affect every visit. Recognition is your first clinical skill.,A diverse elderly patient with a home health nurse. The nurse is leaning forward with active listening posture. A phone interpreter is on the table nearby. ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,The seven categories are: Language — limited English proficiency or a different primary language. Physical — hearing loss. vision impairment. speech difficulties. Gender — care preferences or communication taboos related to gender. Cultural — different beliefs about illness. authority. or disclosure. Emotional — fear. grief. denial. or anxiety blocking the patient's ability to receive information. Perceptual — you and the patient interpret the same event differently. Interpersonal — distrust. past negative healthcare experiences. or power dynamics.,A clean infographic showing seven labeled barrier categories with a visual icon for each one. Medical illustration style on a white background.,A 45-second animated card. Seven numbered barrier icons appear one at a time with a one-sentence definition each. Clean and educational. Each icon uses a distinct color.,45 seconds

ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,A patient nodding does not mean a patient understood. Studies show patients forget forty to eighty percent of what clinicians tell them immediately after the encounter. The teach-back method is the only evidence-based technique that verifies actual comprehension — not just that information was delivered.,A nurse asking a patient to demonstrate how to use an insulin pen. The patient is attempting the demonstration. Focused and realistic interaction. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated split screen. Left: nurse talks — patient nods — question mark appears. Right: nurse asks patient to demonstrate — patient shows correct technique — green checkmark. Text: Teaching ≠ Learning.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,Teach-back in five steps. One: teach in small chunks — one concept at a time. Two: ask the patient to show you. not just confirm. Say: Can you show me how you will do this? Never ask: Do you understand? Three: if they can't demonstrate correctly. simplify. use visuals. and re-explain. Do not blame the patient. Four: repeat until the patient demonstrates correctly. Five: document the outcome.,A clean numbered list of five teach-back steps on a neutral background with a nurse icon demonstrating each step. Educational and professional.,A 45-second step-by-step animation. Five steps appear in sequence. Step 2 highlights the correct question versus the incorrect question in green and red. Step 5 shows documentation.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. You taught insulin pen technique. During teach-back the patient dials 50 units instead of 5. then becomes embarrassed and says he's tired and wants to stop. What do you do now? What do you document? What is the specific safety concern if this patient self-administers tonight?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Thirty-six percent of US adults have basic or below-basic health literacy. For your typical home health patient — elderly. managing multiple conditions. potentially speaking English as a second language — that rate is significantly higher. Your clinical instructions are competing with fear. pain. fatigue. and confusion. Plain language is not a courtesy. It is a clinical obligation.,A home health nurse sitting next to an elderly patient who is looking at a printed instruction sheet with obvious confusion. Warm indoor light. Empathetic interaction. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Stat callout: 36% of US adults have low health literacy. Then an icon of competing factors around a patient: fear pain fatigue confusion. Text: Plain language is clinical care.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Plain language: write and speak at a fifth or sixth grade reading level. Give one instruction at a time. Use active language — say you should take this pill instead of the pill should be taken. Avoid medical jargon. Use visuals and demonstrations. For interpreter services: patients with limited English proficiency have a federal right under Title VI to a qualified interpreter at no cost. Family members may NOT interpret for informed consent. medication instructions. diagnosis. or clinical education.,A nurse holding up a simple illustrated patient instruction card while explaining to an elderly patient. Clear visual communication. Photorealistic. Warm home environment.,A 45-second animation. Plain language do's and don'ts appear. Then a Title VI interpreter rights banner. Family member icon with a red X over clinical content. Agency phone interpreter icon with a green checkmark.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. A patient asks you to review her care plan. She nods throughout. You notice she is holding the instruction sheet upside down. and she has not asked a single question. What does this observation tell you? What do you do next? What do you document?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,The Occupational Safety and Health Act covers you regardless of where you work. A patient's home is your workplace when you are in it. Your employer is required to assess workplace hazards including home environments. provide you with the PPE necessary to work safely. and cannot retaliate against you for raising a safety concern or refusing work that poses an imminent danger.,A home health nurse at the entrance of a patient's home surveying the environment before entering. Professional and alert expression. Suburban neighborhood setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. A home silhouette transforms into a workplace icon. Text: A patient's home is your workplace. OSH Act protections follow you inside.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,Your four OSHA rights are: the right to a safe workplace — your employer must identify and control hazards you encounter in the field. The right to information — you can request a Safety Data Sheet for any chemical you are exposed to. The right to refuse imminently dangerous work — a serious and immediate threat entitles you to refuse without fear of retaliation. And the right to file a confidential complaint with OSHA at 1-800-321-OSHA.,Four shield icons labeled with OSHA rights on a clean white background. Professional safety communication style.,A 45-second animated card. Four OSHA right shields appear in sequence. Shield 3 highlights: Refuse Imminent Danger — No Retaliation. Shield 4 shows the OSHA phone number.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. You arrive and smell a strong chemical odor. The family says they mixed bleach and ammonia to clean. Your eyes are burning. The patient is in the bedroom. What hazard is present? What is the immediate risk to you and the patient? What are your first actions?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,The Globally Harmonized System standardizes how chemical hazards are communicated on labels and Safety Data Sheets. Nine hazard pictograms identify the type of hazard at a glance — flammable. corrosive. toxic. A Safety Data Sheet has sixteen sections. Section eight is the one you use most — it tells you exactly what PPE is required and what the exposure limits are.,A GHS chemical label graphic with nine pictogram icons clearly visible. Professional chemical safety design. Clean educational illustration.,A 30-second animated SDS explainer. Nine GHS pictogram icons appear labeled. SDS document opens to Section 8 highlighted in orange. Text: Section 8 = Your PPE requirements.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,A GHS label has six required elements: product identifier. signal word — danger or warning. hazard statements. precautionary statements. pictograms. and supplier information. In the field. Section 8 of the SDS is your practical reference — it tells you the glove type. respiratory protection level. and eye protection required. If you find an unlabeled container or an unfamiliar chemical in a patient's home. do not use it. Request an SDS or contact poison control at 1-800-222-1222.,A nurse examining an unlabeled spray bottle with a cautious expression before setting it aside and reaching for her phone. Realistic home setting. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated GHS label breakdown. Six label elements appear labeled. Then a field scenario: unlabeled container — nurse sets it aside — calls poison control. Text: When in doubt don't use it.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. A patient hands you an unlabeled spray bottle. She says the doctor used it to clean around the wound last time. The bottle has a faint chemical smell. You don't recognize it. What do you do? What risks are you protecting against? What do you tell the patient?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Incident reporting is not a punitive process. It is the safety system. A near-miss report — something that almost caused harm but didn't — is equally as important as an injury report. because near misses reveal systemic hazards before they injure someone. Your report protects the next employee who faces the same situation.,A nurse submitting an incident report on a tablet with a focused professional expression. Clean office environment visible in the background. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Two icons: Injury report and Near-Miss report — both shown as equally important inputs to a safety system. Text: Your report protects the next worker.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Workplace injury: notify your supervisor immediately — do not wait until the end of your shift. Complete the incident report within twenty-four hours. Seek medical evaluation if the injury requires treatment. Your report triggers the OSHA three-hundred log entry. For medical device reporting: if a device malfunction causes or could cause patient death or serious injury. report to your supervisor immediately. The administrator has ten working days to submit FDA Form 3500A. Do not return or repair the device until risk management clears it.,A flowchart graphic showing workplace injury reporting steps and FDA MDR reporting steps as two parallel pathways. Professional and clean design.,A 45-second two-pathway animation. Left: Workplace injury — Immediate supervisor notification — 24-hour report — OSHA 300 log. Right: Device malfunction — Supervisor — 10 working days — FDA Form 3500A.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. During a transfer assist. the hospital bed rail collapses. The patient falls and has a hip bruise. She refuses to go to the hospital. List your first three immediate actions. What do you document about the device? Is this an MDR-reportable event and why?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,The Patient Bill of Rights is not a mission statement. It is a legally enforceable set of protections under the CMS Conditions of Participation at 42 CFR 484.50. Every patient receives these rights at admission and must be reminded of them on request. You are personally responsible for upholding them at every visit.,A nurse handing a Patient Bill of Rights document to an elderly patient at his kitchen table. Professional and respectful. Warm home setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Patient Bill of Rights document icon with a shield labeled 42 CFR 484.50. Text: Legally enforceable. Not optional. You are responsible.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,Seven core rights in home health. The right to be informed — in their language about their care and diagnosis. The right to participate in care planning. including the right to refuse treatment. The right to privacy and confidentiality. The right to dignity and respect regardless of their condition or behavior. The right to receive care without discrimination. The right to voice grievances without retaliation. And the right to be informed of charges before care begins. Every visit is an opportunity to either uphold or violate these rights.,A clean numbered list infographic showing seven patient rights with a brief label for each. Professional healthcare design.,A 45-second animated card. Seven rights appear sequentially numbered. Each right has a brief scenario icon showing what upholding it looks like in a home health visit.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. The patient says she doesn't want wound care today — she's tired and has visitors coming. At your last visit three days ago. the wound showed early signs of infection. What patient right is at stake? What are your clinical and documentation obligations? Can you proceed without consent?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,An advance directive is the patient's legally recognized voice for a time when they can no longer speak for themselves. Honoring it — even when a family member is pressuring you not to — is both an ethical obligation and a legal requirement. The patient made this decision when they had capacity. Your role is to honor it.,A DNR document on a refrigerator door in a patient's home. Clear and visible. A nurse is noting its location on her tablet. Photorealistic. Clean and sobering.,A 30-second animated card. An advance directive document appears. Family pressure icon with an X. Shield labeled Patient's Voice with a green checkmark. Text: The document controls.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,Know your advance directive types. A DNR means do not attempt CPR — it must be physician-signed and on file. A POLST is more comprehensive and covers intubation. hospitalization. and artificial nutrition decisions. A Living Will contains the patient's specific instructions for end-of-life care. A Healthcare Power of Attorney designates who makes decisions if the patient loses capacity. Your obligations are clear: know whether a directive exists. document its location in every visit note. and never attempt resuscitation if a valid DNR is on file.,Four labeled directive document icons side by side: DNR, POLST, Living Will, Healthcare POA. Clean medical illustration.,A 45-second animated card. Four directive types defined sequentially. Three field obligations appear at the end: Know it — Document its location — Honor it.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. The patient is unresponsive with agonal breathing. A valid physician-signed DNR is on the refrigerator. Her son grabs your arm and says: ignore that paper. save her. she changed her mind. What is the legally and clinically correct response? What do you do and document?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,As a home health worker. you are a mandatory reporter under California law. You are legally required to report suspected abuse. neglect. or exploitation of elderly or dependent adults. The threshold is reasonable suspicion — not proof. You do not investigate. You report. Failure to report when you had reasonable suspicion is a misdemeanor.,A focused home health nurse documenting observations on a tablet after noticing concerning signs on a patient. Serious and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Mandatory reporter badge icon. Threshold meter showing: Proof not required — Suspicion is sufficient. Bold text: Report. Don't investigate.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Physical abuse indicators: unexplained bruising. especially bilateral bruising at the same stage of healing. fractures. burns. and grip marks. Emotional abuse: fearfulness. withdrawal. or visible anxiety when the caregiver is present. Sexual abuse: bruising or injury to genital areas. or patient disclosure. Financial abuse: sudden changes in assets. unpaid bills when resources should be available. a caregiver controlling access to money. Neglect: dehydration. malnutrition. untreated wounds. unsanitary conditions beyond the patient's ability to control. Document what you observe — objectively. factually. and immediately.,A clinical illustration showing observable abuse indicators grouped by type. Medical education style. Neutral and factual. No graphic violence.,A 45-second animated categorized list. Each abuse type appears with observable indicators and brief documentation guidance. Clean and educational tone.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. The patient has bilateral bruises at different stages of healing. She says she bumps into things. Her adult grandson. the primary caregiver. is in the room. She looks at the floor when he speaks and avoids eye contact. List your observations. your suspicion level. and your exact reporting obligations and timeline.,,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,A corporate compliance program exists to prevent. detect. and correct violations before they become legal events. Without a compliance program. a single billing error can become a False Claims Act case. A single undisclosed payment can become an Anti-Kickback violation. Every employee is part of the program — including you.,A professional healthcare compliance meeting with a diverse staff group reviewing documents. Conference room setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Three pillars labeled: Prevent — Detect — Correct. Each shows a relevant scenario icon. Text: Every employee is part of the program.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,The seven OIG elements are: written policies and standards of conduct. a designated Compliance Officer. effective training and education for all employees. open lines of communication including anonymous reporting. internal monitoring and auditing. consistent enforcement and discipline. and prompt corrective action. Your personal role in this program is simple: complete required training. report concerns promptly through authorized channels. and never falsify documentation.,A clean pyramid infographic showing the 7 OIG compliance program elements. Professional corporate compliance design. Clean and educational.,A 45-second animated pyramid build. Seven elements appear from bottom to top. Your role appears at the bottom of the screen: Complete Training — Report Concerns — Never Falsify.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. Your supervisor says: just sign the visit note for last Thursday. We know you were there. The EVV system didn't record it. I need it submitted today for billing. You were at the visit. What is the compliance issue? What do you do?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,Every visit note you complete feeds into a Medicare or Medicaid claim. Every claim is a federal attestation that the care was medically necessary and properly delivered. Rounding up your visit time. Documenting a service you didn't provide. Signing a note without reviewing it. These are not administrative errors — they are potential False Claims Act violations.,A nurse completing a visit note on a tablet with a Medicare claim document visible overlaid in a transparent layer. Symbolic and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Visit note transforms into a Medicare claim. Bold text: Your documentation = a federal attestation. FCA consequence icons appear.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,The False Claims Act imposes civil penalties of thirteen thousand to twenty-six thousand dollars per false claim. plus treble damages. Criminal penalties include up to five years in prison. The Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits anything of value exchanged to induce referrals — this includes gift cards. meals. and favors between employees and vendors. Remember the 60-day rule: if the agency identifies an overpayment from Medicare or Medicaid. it must be returned within sixty days of identification. Keeping an identified overpayment is itself a false claim.,A legal scales icon with FCA dollar amounts on one side and compliance checkmark on the other. Professional legal compliance design.,A 45-second animated card. FCA penalties displayed. AKS examples appear: gift card meal favor — each with a red X. 60-day clock animation for overpayment return.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. Your coworker says she always adds five to seven minutes to her EVV entries. She says the company bills more and everyone does it. Is this fraud. waste. or abuse? What is your obligation? What is the personal risk to your coworker and the risk to the agency?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Multiple federal laws protect employees who report compliance concerns in good faith. The False Claims Act. HIPAA. and OSHA all contain anti-retaliation provisions. You cannot be terminated. demoted. harassed. or have your hours reduced because you made a report. The compliance hotline exists specifically for this purpose.,A nurse confidently picking up a phone to call a compliance hotline. Professional and empowered expression. Clean office setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Three federal law shields: FCA, HIPAA, OSHA. Each shows anti-retaliation icon. Text: You are protected. Report without fear.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Three internal reporting channels: your direct supervisor for general concerns. the Compliance Officer for compliance-specific issues. and the anonymous hotline for any concern where you want confidentiality. External channel: the OIG Hotline at 1-800-HHS-TIPS for fraud involving federal programs. The False Claims Act also contains a qui tam provision — if you bring a lawsuit about fraud against the federal government and it is validated. you may receive fifteen to thirty percent of the government's recovery.,A clean reporting flowchart showing three internal channels and one external channel with labeled icons. Professional compliance communications design.,A 45-second animated reporting channel map. Three internal pathways to a compliance officer icon. External pathway to OIG hotline. Qui tam callout with percentage icon for financial protection.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. Three weeks ago you reported a billing concern through the anonymous hotline. This week your hours were cut thirty percent and you received your first negative performance review in two years. Nothing else changed. Do you have a retaliation claim? What is your evidence? What are your options?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,Healthcare ethics governs decisions where law and policy are silent. ambiguous. or in conflict with each other. The four bioethical principles — autonomy. beneficence. non-maleficence. and justice — provide a framework for the hardest decisions you will face in the field. Learning to apply them before you encounter the situation is what makes the difference.,A home health nurse pausing thoughtfully before entering a patient's room. Contemplative and professional. Warm corridor light. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Four principle icons appear: Autonomy — Beneficence — Non-maleficence — Justice. Text: Ethics applies where policy is silent.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,The four principles are: Autonomy — the patient's right to make decisions about their own care. even ones you disagree with. Beneficence — your duty to act in the patient's best interest. Non-maleficence — your duty to avoid causing harm. including harm from inaction. And Justice — fair. equitable access to care regardless of race. religion. ability to pay. or social status. When principles conflict — most commonly when patient autonomy and non-maleficence are in tension — the Ethics Committee is available for consultation.,Four labeled principle definition cards in a clean grid. Medical ethics education visual style. Professional and neutral.,A 45-second animated card. Four principles defined one at a time with a healthcare home visit scenario for each. Ethics Committee consultation icon appears at the end for conflict resolution.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. A patient with full capacity refuses her prescribed blood thinner. She's afraid of the side effects she read about online. Her husband insists you make sure she takes it. What ethical principle is at stake? What is your obligation to the patient. to the husband. and to the physician?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,An advance directive is the patient's legally recognized voice for a time when they can no longer speak for themselves. Honoring it — even when a family member is pressuring you not to — is both an ethical obligation and a legal requirement. The patient made this decision when they had capacity. Your role is to honor it.,A DNR document displayed on a bedside table next to a patient who is peacefully resting. A nurse is noting its location. Quiet and dignified. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Advance directive icon. Family pressure arrow pointing at the document — a shield blocks it. Text: The patient's voice prevails.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,The most common ethical conflict in home health is a family demanding aggressive intervention when the patient has a valid DNR or POLST. Your resolution framework has four steps. First: honor the directive. Second: call your supervisor and the on-call physician. Third: document the family's statement verbatim — exact words. time. who was present. Fourth: request Ethics Committee consultation if the conflict cannot be resolved immediately. Do not abandon care. Continue comfort measures and attempt to de-escalate the family's distress.,A nurse on the phone in a patient's bedroom. A family member is visible in the background gesturing. Nurse is calm and focused. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated four-step resolution framework. Each step appears numbered. Step 3 highlights documentation: Verbatim — Time — Who was present. Ethics Committee consultation icon at Step 4.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. The patient is deteriorating — altered mental status. labored breathing. mottled extremities. A valid physician-signed DNR is on file. One child says follow the DNR. The other says call 911 and do everything. What do you do? What does the law require? What does ethics require?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Professional boundary violations are not always dramatic. They start small — accepting a gift. a personal phone call. a social media connection — and escalate. Boundaries protect patients from exploitation and workers from liability. The therapeutic relationship depends on a clear professional boundary. Once crossed. it is very difficult to restore.,A professional boundary illustration showing a nurse and patient on opposite sides of a clear professional line. Clean and symbolic. Educational healthcare style.,A 30-second animated card. Small boundary violations appear and escalate: gift card — phone call — social media — financial transaction. Text: Small crossings become large violations.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Boundary violations include accepting money. accepting gifts beyond the agency's policy threshold. connecting with patients on personal social media. providing care for friends or family outside the agency. entering into financial transactions with patients. and any form of sexual contact. The Ethics Committee is available to any employee. patient. or family member who faces an ethical dilemma they cannot resolve independently. Request a consultation through your supervisor or the Compliance Officer. Your consultation is confidential.,A clean labeled list of boundary violation categories on a professional healthcare background. Clear and educational. No graphic content.,A 45-second animated list. Each violation category appears with an X icon. Ethics Committee access path shown as a clear and non-threatening pathway: Supervisor or Compliance Officer. Confidential label.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. A long-term patient you genuinely like and respect hands you one hundred dollars in cash at the end of a visit. She says: this is just a thank-you. you've been so kind for two years. no one has to know. What is the ethical issue? What do you say? What do you document? What happens if you accept?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,Three pathogens drive bloodborne exposure risk in home health: hepatitis B. hepatitis C. and HIV. All three are transmitted through direct contact with infected blood or certain body fluids via a mucous membrane. a needlestick. or non-intact skin. HBV is the most transmissible — a needlestick from an HBV-positive patient carries a thirty percent infection risk without vaccination. Standard precautions prevent exposure to all three.,Three labeled pathogen icons — HBV HCV HIV — on a clean medical background with transmission route labels. Professional medical illustration.,A 30-second animated card. Three pathogen icons appear with risk-per-needlestick percentages. Transmission routes labeled. Standard precautions shield covers all three. Text: One standard. Three protections.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,Transmission by needlestick risk: HBV carries a thirty percent risk per needlestick in an unvaccinated person. HCV carries a 1.8 percent risk. HIV carries 0.3 percent. HBV vaccination is required for healthcare workers — three-dose series. For HCV. there is no vaccine. but early treatment is highly effective. For HIV. there is no cure. but post-exposure prophylaxis started within seventy-two hours is highly effective. These pathogens are not transmitted by saliva alone. tears. sweat. or urine on intact skin. The exposure requires a portal of entry.,A risk comparison infographic showing three pathogens with transmission percentages and vaccine availability indicators. Clean and factual medical design.,A 45-second animated risk comparison. Three columns: HBV — HCV — HIV. Each shows needlestick percentage, vaccine availability, and treatment option. Non-transmission routes listed at bottom.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. During a blood draw. the vacutainer disengages and blood splashes into your eyes. You are not wearing eye protection. The patient's bloodborne pathogen status is unknown. List your immediate response steps in order. What information about the source patient do you need. and why?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,The post-exposure protocol is a timed medical response. Each step has a specific time requirement. and deviation from the sequence reduces treatment effectiveness and creates documentation gaps that can affect workers' compensation claims and legal liability. Know the sequence before you need it.,A nurse washing her hand at a sink immediately after an exposure event. Urgent but controlled demeanor. Clean home health setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. A countdown clock ticking from exposure to 2 hours — 72 hours — showing decreasing effectiveness bars. Text: The protocol is timed. Know it now.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,The five steps. One: immediate first aid. For a needlestick. remove your glove. wash with soap and water for at least thirty seconds. Do not squeeze or try to suck out the wound. For a splash: flush with water for fifteen minutes. Two: call your supervisor immediately — not at the end of the shift. Three: seek medical evaluation at the designated facility within two hours. This is where the PEP decision is made. Four: provide source patient information to facilitate bloodborne pathogen testing if the patient consents. Five: complete the exposure incident report before you leave for the day.,A five-step numbered protocol infographic with timer icons for each step. Clean medical procedure design.,A 45-second animated five-step post-exposure protocol. Each step with time-requirement labels. Step 3 flashes urgency: Within 2 Hours. Step 5 shows completion requirement: Before end of day.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. You step over a used needle on the floor and it punctures through your shoe and nicks your ankle. The patient is on dialysis. You don't know her bloodborne pathogen status. It is 4:45 PM on a Friday. List your first four actions in sequence. What is the time-sensitive factor in this scenario?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Pulmonary tuberculosis is transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei — tiny particles that remain suspended in the air for hours after an infectious person coughs. A surgical mask filters large droplets. It does not filter airborne particles. An N95 respirator filters at least ninety-five percent of airborne particles when properly fitted. This distinction is the difference between protection and exposure.,A side-by-side comparison of a surgical mask and an N95 respirator. Clear and educational. Medical equipment photography.,A 30-second animated card. Surgical mask icon with red X — airborne droplet nuclei pass through. N95 respirator icon with green checkmark — droplet nuclei blocked. Text: Airborne protection requires airborne equipment.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,The active TB symptom cluster: productive cough lasting more than three weeks. night sweats. unexplained weight loss. hemoptysis — blood-tinged sputum — and low-grade fever. High-risk indicators: recent immigration from endemic areas. HIV. diabetes. or shelter exposure. N95 protocol: you must be fit-tested annually. Before every use. perform a seal check — block the valve and breathe in to confirm the mask seals. If you suspect active pulmonary TB and there is no isolation order: don your N95. open windows to increase ventilation. notify your supervisor and the physician immediately. and defer non-urgent procedures until an isolation order is in place.,A clinical illustration showing TB symptom cluster icons with a checklist and an N95 respirator seal-check diagram. Medical education design.,A 45-second animated card. TB symptom checklist builds. N95 seal-check steps animated. Suspected TB response protocol: Don N95 — Open Windows — Notify — Defer non-urgent care.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M11 — TB & Blood Borne Pathogens,Journey/M11/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. Your patient has been coughing for six weeks. Today she coughs blood-tinged sputum in your direction during vital signs. She reports night sweats and has lost twelve pounds. No TB orders are in her chart. You have a surgical mask — not an N95. What do you do right now? What is the risk? Who do you notify and when?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,The FDA's Medical Device Reporting system exists because a device failure is rarely isolated. The same oxygen concentrator model that failed in your patient's home may be deployed in hundreds of other homes. Your MDR report triggers an FDA investigation that can lead to a recall. a safety communication. or a design correction that protects patients across the country.,A home health nurse examining an oxygen concentrator with an alarm indicator showing. Focused and professional. Patient visible in the background. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Single device failure icon spreads to a national map of home patients. FDA investigation icon triggers a recall alert. Text: Your report protects the next patient.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,Three triggers for an MDR. First: the device contributed to or caused a patient death. Second: the device contributed to or caused a serious injury — fractures. burns. significant hemorrhage. hospitalization. Third: the device malfunctioned in a way that could cause death or serious injury if it recurs — even if no harm occurred this time. Devices covered include oxygen concentrators. infusion pumps. hospital beds. patient lifts. glucometers. IV catheters. and wound VAC systems. Malfunction potential alone is a reportable trigger.,A three-trigger decision tree infographic showing MDR reportability criteria. Clean legal-medical design. Professional and factual.,A 45-second animated decision tree. Three MDR triggers appear as branching yes/no questions. Device type examples scroll beneath. Text: Potential matters — actual harm is not required.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. An oxygen concentrator has been alarming for two days. The family silenced it each time. Today the patient has an SpO2 of 78% and is acutely confused. The concentrator appears to have failed. Is this an MDR-reportable event? List your first three actions. What device information do you capture immediately?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,The ten working day deadline for FDA Form 3500A begins when the reportable event is identified. Not when the investigation is complete. Not when the patient is discharged. Not when your supervisor reviews the incident. The identification date is Day Zero — Day Ten is the deadline.,A calendar with Day 0 labeled Identification and Day 10 circled in red. Clean regulatory deadline graphic.,A 30-second animated timeline. Day 0 marked: Event Identified. Clock ticking. Key milestones labeled. Day 10 flashes in red: Deadline — FDA Form 3500A Due.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,The MDR reporting chain has five steps. One: you identify a device event — notify your supervisor immediately and document. Two: supervisor escalates to the Administrator or Risk Manager. Three: Risk Manager confirms reportability through QAPI review. Four: the Administrator submits FDA Form 3500A to the FDA and notifies the manufacturer within ten working days of the identification date. Five: preserve the device — do not return it. repair it. or discard it until risk management releases it. Near-misses can be reported voluntarily using MedWatch Form 3500.,A five-step MDR reporting chain flowchart. Professional regulatory process design with labeled icons for each step.,A 45-second animated reporting chain. Five steps appear sequentially with role labels. Step 5 highlights device preservation with a red stop icon over return and repair actions.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. On Day One you documented a patient fall linked to a bed rail failure. On Day Eight you learn in a QA review that no MDR was initiated. The deadline is Day Ten. Who should have acted by now? What must happen in the next two working days? What is the consequence of missing the deadline?,,, 
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,Your contemporaneous documentation of a device failure event is the primary evidentiary record. It informs the MDR submission. the QAPI investigation. the manufacturer's root cause analysis. and any civil litigation. Document immediately after the event — before you leave the home. before you speak to anyone else. Memory degrades rapidly in the aftermath of an adverse event.,A nurse documenting on a tablet immediately after an incident in a patient's room. Focused and urgent expression. Photorealistic. Clean and professional.,A 30-second animated card. Documentation icon connects to MDR — QAPI — Manufacturer — Litigation icons. Bold text: Document immediately. Before you leave. Before you speak.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,Required documentation elements for a device event. One: device name. manufacturer. model. serial number. and lot number. Two: date. time. and exact location of the event. Three: the exact sequence of the malfunction — what happened in what order. Four: patient status before. during. and after the event. Five: any relevant symptoms from preceding visits. Six: what you did immediately following the event. Seven: who you notified and at what time. If possible. photograph the device before removal. Never re-use a device that was involved in an adverse patient event.,A clinical documentation form for device event reporting with seven numbered fields clearly labeled. Professional medical document design.,A 45-second animated documentation checklist. Seven required elements appear as fields being completed one at a time. Camera icon for photograph. Red X over device re-use icon.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M12 — Medical Device Act,Journey/M12/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,Scenario. A patient lift strap breaks during a transfer. The patient fractures her wrist. In your last three visit notes. you documented that the lift was making a clicking noise. The family reported it to the DME company with no response. What specific information must your documentation include today? How does your prior documentation affect the MDR? What do you do with the device?,,,

"M01-S01","Act 1","S01","Before Sunrise in Quezon City","Quezon City family kitchen — pre-dawn","It is 4:45 in the morning in Quezon City. Marites is already awake. This is not unusual. In the Philippines, the day begins before the sun does. She can hear her mother moving in the kitchen — rice cooker clicking, garlic hitting oil — the sounds of a family that has always started early and worked hard. She folds her scrub top, smooths out the sleeve, and lays it across her nursing bag. On the bag's outer pocket is a small photo: her grandmother standing in front of a mango tree after Sunday Mass. Marites touches it before she does anything else. She is not a new nurse. She has managed post-surgical wounds, administered intravenous medications, and handled difficult family conversations at three in the morning. What is new is the country she is about to work in — and she knows that professional competence and system fluency are two different things.","72","Grounded hopeful","Dissolve from pre-assessment close","Soft cut to lola at table","Photorealistic documentary still of a Filipina woman in navy scrubs sitting in a small pre-dawn kitchen, rice cooker visible, warm incandescent light, cinematic 35mm lens, shallow depth of field, authentic film grain.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope.","anime, cartoon, CGI, plastic skin, distorted hands, extra fingers, watermark, oversaturated HDR, fantasy lighting, stock-photo smile","Medium wide eye-level","Cultural awareness; Workforce inclusion","ACHC CLAS Domain 1; Agency Cultural Competence Policy","LO1","Training Foundations","Pre-shift preparation","N/A","N/A","Narrative setup","Low","N/A","None","Grounds emotional connection before clinical content begins","Low","Mapped","content","","","","","","","",""
"M01-S02","Act 1","S02","The Mano Po Moment","Kitchen doorway — grandmother at table","Her lola — her grandmother — sits at the table already dressed for six o'clock Mass. When Marites enters the kitchen, she bows slightly and takes her grandmother's hand, pressing the back of it gently to her forehead. Mano po, Lola. Her grandmother closes her eyes for a moment, then places her hand on Marites' head in blessing. This is Mano Po — a greeting and a gesture of deep respect that Marites has performed every morning since she was four years old. It is not ceremony. It is how she begins every day: by honoring the person who taught her that other people's dignity is not optional. Her grandmother says quietly: Take care of them the way I know you do. This daily ritual is not separate from Marites' clinical practice. She does not have to be taught to slow down, to soften her language, or to make eye contact without condescension — it is already the grammar of her days.","80","Reverent warm","Soft cut from kitchen scene","Fade to family breakfast table","Photorealistic close documentary shot of Filipina nurse bowing slightly, taking elderly woman's hand and pressing it to her forehead in traditional Mano Po greeting, warm morning kitchen light, 50mm lens, true skin texture.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S03","Act 1","S03","Family Breakfast and Bayanihan","Family dining area — last week home","Breakfast is loud and crowded. Her kuya has already stopped by before his hospital shift. Her tita from next door brought bibingka. Two cousins are arguing about basketball. Nobody was called. Everyone just came. Marites' grandmother grew up in a barangay where Bayanihan was not a concept — it was a physical event. When a family needed to move their bahay kubo — their bamboo home raised on stilts — the entire village would gather unannounced, crouch beneath the structure together, and carry the whole house to its new location on their collective shoulders. Fifteen, twenty men. No one appointed, no one paid. Lifting and moving because the need was visible and the community was the response. When it was done, the family prepared food. That was the entire exchange. Today we carry yours. Tomorrow you carry ours. That is Bayanihan. Not a feeling. A physical act. A village that can lift a house when one family cannot. Marites sits down and her plate is filled before she asks. Her mother says: Kumain ka na — eat now — meaning: you take care of everyone else, so let us take care of you. Nobody cries when the conversation turns to departure. They problem-solve. Her kuya: Keep a printed copy of your license. Do not trust only digital. Her tita: Call us Sundays, we will all be home. Her mother: Eat rice. Even over there. In U.S. healthcare workplaces, Bayanihan instinct can create friction. Unsolicited help across role boundaries can be received as overstepping or scope confusion. Marites will need to translate this instinct — offer support through sanctioned channels, coordinate rather than self-deploy. The spirit stays. The execution adapts.","88","Warm communal","Fade from Mano Po scene","Cut to parol on wall","Photorealistic documentary wide shot of a crowded Filipino family breakfast table, multiple generations, traditional bibingka on table, warm natural morning light through shuttered windows, authentic chaos of communal meal, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S04","Act 1","S04","The Christmas Parol and What Home Sounds Like","Living room — family home","On the living room wall, there is still a parol — the star-shaped Christmas lantern — left from the holiday season. In the Philippines, Christmas begins in September. Not metaphorically. The radio stations switch to carols. The malls put up lights. Families begin planning who will host Noche Buena — the midnight Christmas Eve feast. By December, Simbang Gabi has started — nine consecutive dawn Masses, attended even by people who sleep through the rest of the year. Marites has not missed a single one since she was seven. She pauses at the parol before picking up her bag. She knows she will not be home for the ber months. She will not be at Noche Buena. She will not hear her family sing during Simbang Gabi. She tucks that away somewhere quiet and keeps moving. Workers who migrate for caregiving roles carry invisible emotional burdens. Strong organizational inclusion practices — not just policy posters — create environments where that burden is not compounded by workplace exclusion.","88","Tender sacrificial","Cut from family table","Slow dissolve to bag packing","Photorealistic documentary interior of a modest Filipino living room with a traditional star-shaped parol lantern glowing softly on the wall, family photos, morning light filtering through curtains, 35mm lens, warm authentic tones.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S05","Act 1","S05","Grandmother and the Bracelet","Sala — family living room","Before Marites zips her bag, her grandmother calls her to the sala — the living room. She is holding something small: a thin bracelet woven from coarse thread, the kind sold at the church market after Simbang Gabi. It has been on her grandmother's wrist for forty years. She ties it carefully onto Marites' left wrist and holds both her hands for a moment without speaking. Then: When it gets loud, breathe before you answer. Your patients need you steady, not fast. Marites nods. She does not trust herself to say much. Her grandmother adds: You already know how to take care of people. You learned it at this table. Now go show them. The bracelet will appear again and again throughout this module — during stress, during conflict, during failure, during success. It is the through-line. It is who she is. Emotional regulation is not a soft skill. In home health, rushed responses cause documentation errors, communication failures, missed clinical cues, and unnecessary escalation.","82","Deeply emotional anchored","Dissolve from parol scene","Cut to clinic scene","Photorealistic close-up of elderly Filipino woman's weathered hands tying a simple woven thread bracelet onto a younger woman's wrist, warm soft interior light, shallow depth of field, documentary realism, 85mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S06","Act 1","S06","Marites at Work: The Philippine Clinic","Community health clinic — Quezon City","At her clinic in Quezon City, Marites is the nurse colleagues ask for when a patient interaction is going wrong. Today she is teaching wound care to an elderly patient whose daughter is translating. Marites stops partway through and says gently: Nay, pwede bang ulitin mo sa akin? — Can you repeat that back to me? The patient hesitates, then describes the steps back — correctly, but with one small inversion. Marites does not say wrong. She smiles and says: Almost — let me show you that part once more. When the daughter tries to shortcut and says she got it, Marites says calmly: I just want to make sure for her safety. One more minute. She documents exactly what was explained, what the patient repeated back, and what still needs reinforcement. This is teach-back. It is not a formality. It is the verification mechanism that closes the gap between what was said and what was understood. The wrong answer to whether the patient understood is she nodded. The right answer is a documented description of what the patient demonstrated or repeated back.","90","Warm professional","Cut from bracelet scene","Cut to Po and Opo scene","Photorealistic documentary image of Filipina nurse at bedside in modest Philippine clinic demonstrating wound care to elderly female patient, daughter present, warm fluorescent-balanced light, 35mm lens, authentic clinical setting.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S07","Act 1","S07","Po and Opo — The Language of Respect","Philippine clinic — hallway","Marites never addresses a patient without using po — the Tagalog softening particle that signals respect toward elders and authority. It is so automatic she does not notice it anymore. She calls older women Ma'am or Ate — older sister, even when they are strangers. She calls men Kuya or Sir. She steps back to let elders through doorways. She waits to be seated before sitting. These are not performance behaviors. They are the grammar of respect she was raised speaking. She will arrive in the U.S. and find that some of these signals land differently. A patient might interpret her deference as uncertainty. A colleague might read her careful listening as passivity. A supervisor might not recognize her soft-spoken precision as confidence. She will need to translate not just language, but communication register — and she will need to do it without losing the core values underneath. Every culture has a distinct communication register. Assuming a shared communication code creates patient safety risk.","78","Reflective instructional","Cut from clinic scene","Cut to packing the bag","Photorealistic documentary still of Filipina nurse respectfully stepping aside in a clinic hallway to let an elderly patient pass first, natural fluorescent light, authentic body language, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope.","anime, cartoon, CGI, plastic skin, distorted hands, extra fingers, watermark, oversaturated HDR, fantasy lighting, stock-photo smile","Medium — side angle showing deference in body language","Respectful communication; Cultural awareness; Implicit bias","ACHC CLAS Standard 5; Cultural Competence Policy","LO1|LO3","Communication","Cross-cultural communication register adaptation","N/A","N/A","Cultural teaching","Moderate","N/A","None","Bridges Filipino respect culture to CLAS-compliant adaptive communication","Moderate","Mapped","content","","","","","","","",""
"M01-S08","Act 1","S08","Packing the Bag","Bedroom — night before departure","The night before departure, Marites packs with the same precision she uses for a complex visit. Nursing license. Employment authorization. Credential evaluations. Vaccination records. Three copies of everything. Her kuya organized it all into labeled folders — because that is what family does. At the bottom of the bag, her mother puts a small container of sinigang powder and a photograph from her clinic. So you remember what competence looks like, she says — without irony. Marites wraps the bracelet in a clean cloth so it does not catch on anything during the flight. She is not sentimental. She is prepared. Documentation preparation is risk preparation. In clinical onboarding, missing credentials create delayed clearance and unsafe staffing. In field practice, missing records create care gaps. The habit of completeness starts before the shift, before the flight, before the first patient contact.","70","Determined composed","Cut from Po and Opo scene","Cut to airport departure","Photorealistic documentary overhead shot of open suitcase with nursing license documents, labeled folders, and small jar of sinigang spice mix, warm bedroom lamp light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S09","Act 1","S09","Airport: The Goodbye That Does Not Ask for Crying","Ninoy Aquino International Airport — departure gate","At Ninoy Aquino International Airport, the goodbye is practical and full. Her mother re-checks her boarding pass. Her kuya hands her a local SIM card and tells her to text when she lands. Her tita slips a rosary into her jacket pocket. Her grandmother holds her hand and does not let go until the last possible moment — then says simply: Alis na. Go now. There is no dramatic speech. Filipino goodbyes are often like this: matter-of-fact on the outside, enormous on the inside. Emotion is not performed. It is carried. Marites touches the bracelet. Picks up her bag. Walks through the gate. The learner must feel this moment — not as tragedy, but as the specific dignity of someone choosing to leave everything familiar because service is that important to them. This is who Marites is. This is what is at stake when she is dismissed, interrupted, or excluded later in the story.","75","Sacrificial dignified","Cut from packing","Dissolve to U.S. airport arrival","Photorealistic documentary wide shot of Filipina nurse at airport departure gate embracing family, restraint in expressions, warm airport lighting, 35mm lens, authentic emotional realism.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S10","Act 1","S10","Landing: The First Cultural Shock","U.S. airport — arrivals hall and bus","The airport in the United States is large, efficient, and impersonal. Nobody helps without being asked first. Nobody makes eye contact unless they need something. The signage is clear. The process is fast. Nobody lingers. In the Philippines, airports are loud with reunions. Here, arrivals walk briskly and separately. She takes the bus to her temporary housing. The driver does not respond to her greeting. Not rudely — he just does not respond. She files that away. Different system. Her first evening: she unpacks, eats a Cup Noodles because the grocery run can wait, and calls her family on video chat. Her grandmother is already asleep. Her mother holds the phone up anyway so she can see the parol still on the wall. She keeps the video open until the data connection drops. Culture shock is not weakness. It is the cognitive load of recalibrating every social and professional assumption simultaneously. For healthcare workers, unmanaged culture shock can affect communication quality, documentation accuracy, and patient relationship-building.","85","Isolating observant","Dissolve from airport goodbye","Cut to first week EHR scene","Photorealistic documentary image of Filipina woman alone in large efficient U.S. airport arrivals area, brisk solo travelers around her, quiet contrast to Philippine warmth, 35mm lens, natural lighting.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S11","Act 1","S11","First Week: The System Is Different","Agency — nursing station and EHR workstation","The EHR system has twelve required fields she has never seen. The abbreviations are different from the ones she trained on. The handoff format is faster and more verbal — less written, more assumed. In the Philippines, a ward handoff included written notes, verbal confirmation, and physical bedside assessment. Here, the expectation is a ten-minute verbal briefing and a chart review. The first time she asks a clarifying question during handoff, the charge nurse glances at the clock. Not unkindly — but the signal is clear: brevity is currency here. She writes everything down. She stays an extra twenty minutes reviewing charts before leaving. She does not ask questions she can answer herself. She saves her questions for the ones that matter. Adapting to a faster handoff culture does not mean abandoning closed-loop communication. It means executing it efficiently. One targeted clarifying question, timed correctly, is more valuable than ten vague ones at the wrong moment.","82","Careful adaptive","Cut from landing scene","Cut to grocery store scene","Photorealistic documentary shot of Filipina nurse writing in notebook at nursing station while reviewing EHR screen with unfamiliar documentation fields, fluorescent office light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S12","Act 1","S12","First Grocery Store and Small Shocks","Local grocery store — off day","She goes to the grocery store on her day off. She spends twenty minutes looking for garlic rice. She cannot find it. She settles for white rice and garlic from the produce section. She brings everything to the cashier and says: Good morning, Ma'am — and the cashier, without looking up, says: You have a rewards card? Not rude. Just transactional. In the Philippines, strangers at market stalls ask where you are going, who your family is, whether you have eaten. The cashier is doing her job efficiently. Marites is grieving a style of warmth she did not know she needed. She buys her groceries and walks back to her apartment. She texts her lola a photo of the white rice. Her lola responds with three rice emojis and a laughing face. She laughs alone in her apartment and feels slightly better. Clinical relationships in American home health are professional and boundaried — not cold, but structured. Knowing this difference allows the clinician to adapt without misreading professional distance as hostility.","78","Wry tender","Cut from EHR scene","Cut to resilience scene","Photorealistic documentary still of Filipina woman alone in a large American grocery store aisle looking at plain white rice bags, fluorescent store lighting, subtle expression of quiet humor and homesickness, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S13","Act 1","S13","Resilience in Practice","Agency — break room and hallway","In the Philippines, Marites has worked through a typhoon warning, a dengue outbreak in her barangay, and a hospital generator failure during a night shift. She kept working. She figured out what was needed and she did it. Filipino resilience — the cultural norm of maintaining a positive face and continuing to function under pressure — is not denial. It is a survival skill that her community practices so consistently it becomes professional reflex. Here, she is watching colleagues express frustration openly — at the system, at the scheduler, at the EHR — in ways she was trained to absorb quietly. She notices that here, speaking up is not the same as complaining. It is sometimes how the system gets fixed. She is building a new operational vocabulary, and she is doing it deliberately. Compliance and safety culture in ACHC-accredited agencies depend on staff who report concerns, document anomalies, and escalate without waiting for permission. Speaking up is not disloyalty — it is the job.","80","Resilient observant","Cut from grocery scene","Cut to agency orientation","Photorealistic documentary scene of Filipina nurse in U.S. agency break room observing colleagues expressing frustration, her expression calm and observational, realistic office environment, natural light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S14","Act 1","S14","Agency Orientation: Reading the Policies with New Eyes","Agency conference room — orientation day","At agency orientation, Marites is given a thick binder. She reads it the way she prepared for licensing exams — front to back, with a highlighter. She marks: Language Access. Interpreter Services Required. Patient Rights. Anti-Discrimination. Reporting Obligations. Anti-Retaliation. In her Philippine clinic, many of these existed as values rather than written operational standards. Here they are legal obligations with documented workflows, survey traceability, and corrective action pathways. The commitment is the same. The architecture is more formal. She reads the Anti-Retaliation clause twice. She has never worked somewhere that explicitly wrote down that she could not be punished for reporting a concern. She finds this remarkable. ACHC accreditation requires that agencies not only have these policies but demonstrate evidence that staff understand and apply them. Orientation is the beginning of audit-traceable competency documentation. Staff who read carefully and ask questions are building defensibility.","82","Alert composed","Cut from resilience scene","Cut to first handoff","Photorealistic documentary image of Filipina nurse at orientation table reading agency policy binder with yellow highlighter, realistic conference room, overhead warm lighting, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S15","Act 1","S15","First Handoff: A New Rhythm","Agency — nursing station hallway","Her first full team handoff is Thursday morning. The charge nurse moves through patient assignments in fifteen minutes. Allergy flags. Visit priorities. Documentation holds. Insurance authorizations. Interpreter requests pending. Marites listens, writes, and maps each patient against what she already reviewed in the chart. When a detail is unclear — a wound classification she does not recognize — she raises her hand and asks one targeted question. The charge nurse answers without stopping her pace. Marites writes it down. The handoff ends. Aldrin — the experienced clinician she has been paired with for the week — catches up with her in the hallway: Good catch on the classification. Most people let that one go. She knows she caught it because she prepared the night before. Closed-loop handoff is a safety mechanism, not a social convention. One targeted clarifying question, timed correctly, is more valuable than ten vague ones at the wrong moment.","75","Alert prepared","Cut from orientation","Cut to rights board scene","Photorealistic documentary shot of clinical morning huddle with nurse writing in notebook while charge nurse reviews assignments at nursing station, realistic fluorescent lighting, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S16","Act 1","S16","The Rights Board: Rules Become Real","Agency hallway — patient coordination area","In the hallway outside the patient coordination room, there is a laminated board. Patient rights. Language access. Interpreter services at no charge. Anti-discrimination protections. Grievance process. Marites stops and reads it as if she has never seen policies before — because here, they are the operational landscape she will navigate daily. She notices: interpreter services are explicitly required, not suggested. Family members may not substitute for qualified interpretation in clinical decisions. This is different from what she saw in her previous work environment, where family interpretation was common practice driven by necessity. She photographs the board on her personal phone. Not for evidence — for study. The policies posted in an ACHC-accredited agency are operational standards surveyors will evaluate during review. Every field worker is expected to know them, apply them, document them, and escalate when they are not followed.","72","Alert professional","Cut from handoff scene","Cut to pre-visit prep","Photorealistic documentary close-up of laminated patient rights and language access policy board on agency wall, realistic institutional setting, balanced overhead light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S17","Act 1","S17","Pre-Visit Preparation: First Patient","Agency parking lot — car before visit","Before driving to her first solo visit, Marites reviews the patient chart, checks language preference, identifies the interpreter contact number, reviews allergies and risk markers, and rehearses the patient's name. She says it aloud three times: Henderson. Mr. Henderson. She checks her watch, calculates her drive time, and notes that she has a five-minute window before the appointment to compose herself and review her teaching plan. She touches her bracelet. She knocks. Pre-visit preparation is a patient safety habit. Reviewing language access needs, allergy flags, communication preferences, and care plan priorities before arrival — not during — reduces the cognitive load at the door and gives the clinician the space to be fully present with the patient.","65","Focused calm","Cut from rights board","Cut to challenge 1","Photorealistic documentary image of Filipina nurse in parked car reviewing tablet chart before patient visit, morning light through windshield, bracelet visible, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S18-Q","Act 1","S18-Q","Challenge 1: Cultural Preference vs Clinical Urgency — Question","Mr. Henderson home — front door","Help Marites make the correct operational decision. The wound may be deteriorating. The patient cannot speak to confirm or deny the accommodation request. Marites has four options. What is the most defensible immediate action? Option B: Respect the family's preference completely by leaving the home and messaging the office to reschedule with a different clinician.
