"M01-S18-D","Act 1","S18-D","Challenge 1 Debrief: Rights and Urgency Are Not a Choice","Debrief card","Operational Case Review
1) Correct decision: Option A is correct because it preserves patient safety and workflow integrity under pressure.
2) Why correct: Acknowledge the family's request, rapidly assess wound urgency at the bedside, call the supervisor immediately for accommodation routing, and document both the preference and the clinical findings.
3) Incorrect option analysis:
- Option B risk: Respect the family's preference completely by leaving the home and messaging the office to reschedule with a different clinician.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option C risk: Proceed with wound care because clinical urgency overrides accommodation requests when deterioration is present.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option D risk: Ask the family to sign a refusal form first, then determine next steps based on available staffing.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
4) Patient safety implications: uncontrolled communication barriers or delayed escalation can compound into harm.
5) Workflow implications: sequence matters; right actions in the wrong order still produce risk.
6) Documentation implications: chart objective findings, what was verified, what was escalated, and who received handoff.
7) Escalation implications: trigger supervisor pathway when unresolved clinical, communication, or conduct risk remains.
8) Survey implications: ACHC/CMS reviewers focus on evidence chain, not intent.
9) Operational consequences: unresolved gaps can lead to adverse events, corrective action, and loss of trust.
10) Disciplinary/legal/defensibility: omissions and unsupported charting increase disciplinary risk and weaken legal defense.

The correct answer is A. In home health, you will face moments where two legitimate obligations pull in opposite directions. The defensible response is never to choose one and abandon the other. Option A is correct because it holds both simultaneously — urgency assessment at bedside, supervisor escalation for accommodation routing, and complete documentation of the preference, the clinical findings, and the plan. Option B abandons the patient at the moment of highest clinical risk. A wound deteriorating with no assessment on record is a patient safety failure, regardless of how respectful the departure was. Option C overrides an accommodation process the patient has a legal right to access. Proceeding without attempting accommodation — even in clinical urgency — creates survey exposure and trust rupture. Documentation that appears to override rights without process is a compliance liability. Option D inverts the correct sequence. Paperwork before urgency assessment is a workflow error with direct patient harm potential. The rule that holds across every challenge in this module: assess urgency first, escalate immediately, document both the preference and the clinical findings, and let your supervisor route the solution. You do not carry the accommodation decision alone. That is what escalation is for.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Dissolve to Act 2","Photorealistic documentary image of nurse on phone outside residential home, supervisor call in progress, chart open, bracelet visible, natural morning light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. The correct answer is B. Option A fails the language access standard for clinical teaching and creates a documentation problem. A note saying education completed when comprehension was never verified is not defensible during a survey review — and it is not safe for the patient. Option C creates a fragmented education record. The most dangerous teaching is teaching that was partially delivered before the communication barrier was controlled. A patient who heard half an explanation and remembered pieces of it is more hazardous than a patient who received no teaching yet. Option D substitutes a signature for comprehension. A signature is not evidence of understanding. It is a form. Option B is correct because it controls the communication barrier before education begins, uses a qualified interpreter who meets the professional standard for clinical accuracy, performs teach-back to verify what was understood, and documents the barrier, the interpreter ID, the method, and the patient's demonstrated comprehension. That chain is what ACHC surveyors will look for. It is also what protects the patient from an insulin dosing error that begins with an assumption.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Cut to consequence scene","Photorealistic debrief image — nurse on interpreter phone call with patient in realistic home setting, chart visible, natural light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. 2) Why correct: Calmly address the behavior in the moment, then submit a formal report to the supervisor with the exact behavior, witnesses, time, location, and an anti-retaliation request.
3) Incorrect option analysis:
- Option B risk: Wait until after shift and report it to HR the following morning to avoid making the situation worse right now.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option C risk: Confront the coworker loudly in the break room to make clear the behavior is unacceptable.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option D risk: Focus on patient care and avoid getting involved in personnel issues — the workplace environment is not her responsibility to correct.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
4) Patient safety implications: uncontrolled communication barriers or delayed escalation can compound into harm.
5) Workflow implications: sequence matters; right actions in the wrong order still produce risk.
6) Documentation implications: chart objective findings, what was verified, what was escalated, and who received handoff.
7) Escalation implications: trigger supervisor pathway when unresolved clinical, communication, or conduct risk remains.
8) Survey implications: ACHC/CMS reviewers focus on evidence chain, not intent.
9) Operational consequences: unresolved gaps can lead to adverse events, corrective action, and loss of trust.
10) Disciplinary/legal/defensibility: omissions and unsupported charting increase disciplinary risk and weaken legal defense.

The correct answer is A. Option A is correct because it does two things at once: it stops the behavior in real time and it creates a defensible formal record. Calm, direct, in-the-moment correction is not aggression — it is professionalism applied at the right moment. The formal report with objective behavioral detail is what makes the correction traceable, investigable, and protected from retaliation. Option B delays correction and weakens the record. Memory fades overnight. Witnesses may not recall details the next morning. The behavior continues in the gap. Option C is incorrect because aggressive confrontation creates a second conduct issue and muddies the reporting process. When an incident becomes a dual-conduct conflict, the original behavior becomes harder to address cleanly. Option D is the most dangerous answer. Silence normalizes exclusion behavior. Workforce disrespect compounds over time — it erodes team trust, impairs communication safety, and eventually touches patient care. The correct standard in an ACHC-accredited agency: see it, address it, document it, escalate it. Anti-retaliation protections exist specifically so that staff can report without fear. Using them is not weakness — it is the job.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Cut to supervisor coaching scene","Photorealistic documentary image of nurse writing formal incident report at desk, detailed notes visible, professional composed expression, realistic office setting, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S28-D","Act 2","S28-D","Challenge 4 Debrief: Defensible Correction Has a Sequence","Debrief card","Operational Case Review
1) Correct decision: Option A is correct because it preserves patient safety and workflow integrity under pressure.
2) Why correct: Create a late-entry addendum for each record with a timestamp, objective detail including cultural preference and interpreter information, and notify the supervisor about the pattern.
3) Incorrect option analysis:
- Option B risk: Go back into the original note text and rewrite it to include the missing information so the record appears complete and consistent.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option C risk: Add a brief note at the end of each record saying 'patient understands' and move forward.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option D risk: Leave both records as they are and document the missing information fully at the next visit.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
4) Patient safety implications: uncontrolled communication barriers or delayed escalation can compound into harm.
5) Workflow implications: sequence matters; right actions in the wrong order still produce risk.
6) Documentation implications: chart objective findings, what was verified, what was escalated, and who received handoff.
7) Escalation implications: trigger supervisor pathway when unresolved clinical, communication, or conduct risk remains.
8) Survey implications: ACHC/CMS reviewers focus on evidence chain, not intent.
9) Operational consequences: unresolved gaps can lead to adverse events, corrective action, and loss of trust.
10) Disciplinary/legal/defensibility: omissions and unsupported charting increase disciplinary risk and weaken legal defense.

The correct answer is A. Option B is the most dangerous answer in this challenge. Going back into the original note and rewriting it is record alteration. It destroys chronological integrity, creates legal exposure, and in a survey context can constitute falsification. If an auditor or surveyor compares electronic metadata with note content and finds they do not align, the consequences extend far beyond the two missing fields. Option C is the most common wrong answer — not because it is aggressive, but because it is vague. Patient understands is not a clinical finding. It is an assertion. It tells no one what was taught, how understanding was verified, what the patient demonstrated back, or what still needs reinforcement. Option D delays correction into a different visit with a different clinical context, leaving the existing gap open and the care team acting on incomplete information in the meantime. Option A is correct because it does three things: it preserves record integrity by creating a transparent late-entry with a timestamp, it adds objective clinical detail that actually means something to the next clinician reading the chart, and it escalates the pattern to a supervisor and QA so the workflow gap can be corrected at the system level. Defensible documentation is not about length. It is about specificity, objectivity, completeness, and correct sequence.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Cut to mentor defensibility lesson","Photorealistic documentary image of nurse reviewing completed compliant addendum entry on EHR screen, timestamps visible, natural office light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S29","Act 2","S29","Mentor Lesson: Survey Defensibility","Conference alcove","Aldrin sits with Marites over a coffee and explains something she needs to understand before her first independent shift. Surveyors do not grade intentions. They do not care that you meant to do the right thing. They review evidence chains: risk was recognized, action was taken, escalation was completed, and documentation shows exactly what happened and when. If any link in that chain is missing, the rest does not matter. A well-intentioned clinician with incomplete documentation is indistinguishable from a careless one in a survey record. That is why documentation is not bureaucracy. It is the proof that you did what you said you did.","52","Authoritative mentoring","Cut from challenge 4 debrief","Cut to near-miss escalation","Photorealistic documentary image of mentor and nurse in quiet alcove with coffee, reviewing documentation checklist, realistic warm light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. The correct answer is A. Option B — correct now, document later — is one of the most common documentation errors in home health. End-of-day documentation of a same-visit near-miss is memory-dependent, continuity-fragmented, and legally weaker than a same-visit record. If another clinician visits this patient tonight or tomorrow morning before your documentation is complete, they will act on the old conflicting instructions. Option C transfers clinical responsibility to a family member. Monitoring medication intake is not a family surveillance task — it is a clinical safety function that requires a clinician's judgment, not a worried family member's observation. Option D waits for a physician order update before correcting a patient who is actively at risk of dosing error. That is a delay with a direct harm pathway. Option A is correct because it acts in the correct sequence: correct the patient at the point of care, escalate to the supervising clinician during the same visit so the order can be clarified, and document the near-miss with the correction, the teach-back result, and the updated care plan before you leave the home. Near-miss documentation is not punishment. It is a safety tool that closes the risk loop and protects the next clinician who opens this chart.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Cut to grievance trigger","Photorealistic documentary debrief image — nurse completing same-visit documentation with corrected medication schedule visible on screen, natural kitchen light, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. Option D waits for a physician order update before correcting a patient who is actively at risk of dosing error. That is a delay with a direct harm pathway. Option A is correct because it acts in the correct sequence: correct the patient at the point of care, escalate to the supervising clinician during the same visit so the order can be clarified, and document the near-miss with the correction, the teach-back result, and the updated care plan before you leave the home. Near-miss documentation is not punishment. It is a safety tool that closes the risk loop and protects the next clinician who opens this chart."

"M01-S40-Q","Act 3","S40-Q","Challenge 6: Integrated Workflow Sequencing — Question","Patient home — complex visit","Help Marites sequence the visit correctly. She also has not yet confirmed language preference or activated interpretation. She has four options. What is the most defensible sequence for this visit? Option A: Assess the pain indicator immediately at bedside, confirm language preference and activate the qualified interpreter, explain the interpreter's role to the patient, deliver teach-back after teaching, document all findings and the interpreter ID, and escalate any unresolved clinical risk before leaving. Option B: Begin education immediately since the family is ready and the interpreter can be added if confusion appears during teaching. Option C: Escalate to your supervisor before any bedside clinical activity to avoid personal liability for unexpected findings. "M01-S40-D","Act 3","S40-D","Challenge 6 Debrief: Right Steps, Right Order","Debrief card","Operational Case Review
1) Correct decision: Option A is correct because it preserves patient safety and workflow integrity under pressure.
2) Why correct: Assess the pain indicator at bedside, confirm language preference and activate the qualified interpreter, deliver teach-back after teaching, document all findings and interpreter ID, and escalate any unresolved clinical risk.
3) Incorrect option analysis:
- Option B risk: Begin education immediately since the family is ready — add the interpreter only if confusion appears during teaching.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option C risk: Escalate to your supervisor before any bedside clinical activity to avoid personal liability for unexpected findings.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
- Option D risk: Build rapport with the patient first through casual conversation and delay both the clinical assessment and documentation until the relationship is established.. Looks reasonable under pressure, but creates a preventable documentation and escalation gap.
4) Patient safety implications: uncontrolled communication barriers or delayed escalation can compound into harm.
5) Workflow implications: sequence matters; right actions in the wrong order still produce risk.
6) Documentation implications: chart objective findings, what was verified, what was escalated, and who received handoff.
7) Escalation implications: trigger supervisor pathway when unresolved clinical, communication, or conduct risk remains.
8) Survey implications: ACHC/CMS reviewers focus on evidence chain, not intent.
9) Operational consequences: unresolved gaps can lead to adverse events, corrective action, and loss of trust.
10) Disciplinary/legal/defensibility: omissions and unsupported charting increase disciplinary risk and weaken legal defense.

The correct answer is A. Defensible care is sequence-dependent. Right steps in the wrong order still produce risk. Option B begins education before the communication barrier is controlled and before a potential pain symptom is assessed. This creates two simultaneous gaps: unverified comprehension and an uninvestigated clinical finding. Teaching that proceeds before a pain indicator is assessed and before an interpreter is activated is not efficient — it is incomplete. Option C escalates before bedside assessment. This is premature escalation without clinical information. Your supervisor cannot make an informed clinical decision about an unassessed finding. Your job is to assess first, then escalate with findings. Option D delays both clinical assessment and documentation in favor of rapport building. Rapport matters. But an unassessed pain indicator and an uncontrolled language barrier do not wait for comfort. Option A is correct because it executes in the correct order: identify and respond to the clinical finding first, control the communication environment second, deliver and verify the teaching third, and close the visit with complete documentation and any necessary escalation. Sequence is not bureaucracy. Sequence is how you prevent compounded errors.","95","Operational case-review coaching","Answer reveal","Cut to independent shift prep","Photorealistic debrief image showing nurse with completed visit sequence checklist beside patient chart, realistic home setting, 35mm lens.","Character anchor: Marites, Filipina, early 30s, tied-back dark hair, navy scrubs, woven bracelet left wrist, calm eyes, consistent badge and stethoscope. "M01-S47","Act 3","S47","Final Debrief and Competency Confirmation","Final debrief card","You did not pass by guessing. You passed by sequencing. That is the operational definition of cultural competence — not performance, but practiced precision applied with consistent respect. The learner who completes this module carries three things forward: the knowledge that every clinical decision has an evidence chain that needs to exist in the record; the skill to activate interpreter workflow, perform teach-back, escalate correctly, and document defensibly; and the understanding that cultural competence is not a training badge. ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"Cultural competence is the ability to deliver effective care to patients with different cultural backgrounds, values, and communication styles. The CLAS Standards — fifteen federal benchmarks — define what equitable care looks like in home health. This is not a soft skill. It is a survey-ready, patient-safety requirement.",A diverse home health team of nurses and aides in professional scrubs gathered outside a residential home. Warm daylight. Photorealistic. Professional and welcoming.,A 30-second 2D animated intro card. A diverse group of patient icons surrounded by cultural symbols — language bubbles prayer symbols family structures. Bold text: Cultural Competence = Patient Safety.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"The CLAS Standards have three domains. First: governance and workforce — your agency must build cultural competence into hiring, training, and leadership. Second: language assistance — patients with limited English proficiency must receive qualified interpreter services at no cost, not a family member translation. Third: accountability — cultural accommodations must be documented in the clinical record.",A home health nurse reviewing a care plan with an interpreter on a phone while sitting with an elderly patient from a South Asian background. Photorealistic. Warm and professional.,A 45-second explainer animation. Three labeled icons expand in sequence: Governance — Language Assistance — Accountability. Each shows a real-world home health scenario example.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Time for a scenario. You arrive for wound care. The patient's daughter says her mother will not allow a male caregiver to provide personal care due to religious beliefs. The patient agrees. The wound needs attention. What are your next steps? Think about patient rights, CLAS Standards, and what you document.",,, 
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"Culture shapes how your patients communicate with you — or whether they communicate at all. Eye contact that signals respect in one culture signals aggression in another. Silence may mean agreement, or shame, or confusion. In some cultures, health decisions are made by the family, not the patient. Recognizing these patterns is the first step to effective care.",A male home health nurse sitting across from an elderly female patient. He uses open body language and a calm expression. Natural warm indoor light. Photorealistic.,A 30-second card showing cultural communication patterns side-by-side — direct eye contact with checkmark for one culture and an X for another. Clean 2D animation.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"Three rules for cross-cultural communication. First: use open body language and a neutral tone — avoid assumptions about what signals mean. Second: verify comprehension with teach-back — ask the patient to explain back or demonstrate, never accept a nod as understanding. Third: for patients with limited English, use your agency-approved interpreter service. Family members must not interpret clinical content.",A nurse using a phone interpreter while demonstrating a medication technique to a patient. Professional and focused. Photorealistic. Home setting with natural light.,A 45-second animated rule card. Three numbered rules appear in sequence with visual demonstrations of each. Rule 3 shows a phone interpreter icon versus a family member icon with a red X.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Here is your scenario. You are teaching insulin pen technique. The patient nods and says yes throughout. He speaks limited English. When you ask him to demonstrate, he holds the pen incorrectly. What do you do, and what do you document?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"Cultural bias is unconscious. It affects who you spend more time with, who you assume understands less, who you assume is non-compliant. Workplace discrimination is when bias drives an action — assigning a patient away, refusing to enter a home, treating one family differently than another. Both are your professional responsibility to recognize and address.",A reflective photo of a home health nurse looking in a mirror with a thoughtful expression. Symbolizing self-awareness. Clean and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated video. A bias icon transitions to an action icon. Text: Bias is unconscious. Discrimination is a choice. Address both.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"The EEOC prohibits discrimination in employment based on race, national origin, religion, sex, age, and disability. If a patient or family directs discriminatory language or behavior toward you or a colleague, you are obligated to document it objectively and report to your supervisor and HR. Retaliation for making a good-faith report is separately prohibited under federal law.",A professional HR meeting in a bright office. A home health nurse is speaking with an HR manager across a table with a notepad. Photorealistic. Professional tone.,A 45-second animated explainer. EEOC shield icon with six protected categories listed. Then a flowchart: Observe — Document objectively — Report to Supervisor and HR — No Retaliation.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M01 — Cultural Awareness,Journey/M01/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. Your coworker mutters to you about a patient — these people never follow instructions, it's their culture. The patient is in the next room. You are the only witness. What is your professional obligation? What do you do next?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"The Agency Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan exists so that when a disaster strikes, every employee knows their role. You are not expected to figure it out in the moment. Your job is to know the plan before the emergency arrives, and execute it when it does. This lesson covers your specific role as a field worker.",An aerial view of a neighborhood with an emergency response vehicle visible. A home health nurse is on her phone looking at a clipboard. Dramatic natural light. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated intro. Map view of a neighborhood with emergency alert icons appearing. Text: Know your role before the emergency arrives.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"When an emergency is declared, your first four steps are: stop non-urgent visits, contact your supervisor immediately, attempt to contact every patient on your schedule and document every attempt, and follow the agency communication tree. Do not assume someone else made contact with your patients. Document every call with the time and outcome.",A home health nurse on the phone with a clipboard in her car during a visible emergency situation. Focused and professional. Photorealistic. Overcast dramatic sky visible through car window.,A 45-second animated sequence showing 4 numbered steps. Each step has an icon and a brief action label. Step 4 shows the agency communication tree chain.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You receive a shelter-in-place order at 6:15 AM. Four patients are scheduled. Your supervisor does not answer on the first call. List your actions in order. What do you document? When do you escalate and to whom?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"Home health agencies use a four-class triage system for emergencies. Class One patients are life-sustaining technology dependent — ventilators, infusion pumps, oxygen. They are contacted first. Class Two patients have significant medical needs. Class Three have moderate needs. Class Four can manage independently. You should know your patients' triage class before an emergency happens.",An infographic-style illustration of four home health patients each representing a different triage class. Icons showing medical equipment dependency. Clean professional graphic.,A 35-second animated card. Four patient icons labeled Class I through IV with brief labels and color coding. Clock icons show contact time requirements for each class.,35 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"Class One: technology-dependent patients must be contacted within thirty minutes of emergency activation. These patients cannot survive without power, supplies, or clinical support. Class Two: significant medical needs, contact within one hour. Class Three: stable patients, contact within four hours. Class Four: independent. For evacuation, your role is to facilitate and coordinate with emergency services. You do not transport patients yourself.",A home health coordinator on a phone with a triage list on a tablet. Emergency vehicles visible through a window. Professional and focused. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animation showing each class with a countdown timer. Class I shows a ventilator icon with 30-minute clock. Evacuation scene shows nurse coordinating with paramedics — not driving a patient.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Wildfire evacuation order. Five patients: A is on a home ventilator. B is ambulatory with stable wound care. C has dementia and lives alone. D has already refused to evacuate. E has her daughter present and available. In what order do you contact them, and what special action applies to each?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"During an emergency, you are still legally required to document. Systems may be down. Your EMR may be unavailable. But the documentation obligation does not disappear — it shifts to paper. What you write during an emergency becomes the legal and clinical record of what happened to every patient under your care.",A nurse writing on a paper form in a car during a stormy day. Professional attire. Clipboard and pen in hand. A mobile phone on the seat showing the agency number. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. EMR screen goes offline with an X — paper form appears with a checkmark. Text: The obligation doesn't disappear. It shifts.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"Document every contact attempt with timestamps. Document patient status at the time of contact. Document care provided or deferred and why. If a patient was moved, document their new location. Document all instructions given to the patient or family. Use the agency paper backup form. Sign and date every page. Transfer everything to the EHR within twenty-four hours of system restoration.",A close-up of a nurse's hands filling out a paper emergency backup form with a pen. Clock visible in the background showing the time. Clean professional composition. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated checklist. Each required documentation element appears with a checkbox. Final frame: Transfer to EHR within 24 hours of system restoration.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M02 — Emergency & Disaster Preparedness,Journey/M02/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"The EHR is down. You completed wound care on a Class Two patient — new infection signs. You attempted two other patients with no answer. Using paper backup, what fields do you document for each event? What happens to this documentation when the system comes back online?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"A complaint, a grievance, and an allegation are three different types of events, each requiring a different response. Your job as a field worker is not to investigate. It is to receive the concern, document it accurately, and submit it to the right person without delay.",A calm home health nurse listening attentively to an upset family member at a patient's doorway. Empathetic and professional body language. Photorealistic. Natural indoor light.,A 30-second animation showing three labeled pathways: Complaint — Grievance — Allegation. Each branches to a different required response. Clean professional 2D style.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"A complaint is an informal concern about service quality — the nurse was late, the visit was too short. You address what you can, document it, and submit it to your supervisor. A grievance is a formal allegation that patient rights were violated. It requires a documented intake, administrative review, and a written response within ten working days. An allegation is suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation. It requires immediate mandatory reporting under state law. Suspicion is sufficient. You do not need proof.",A split-screen comparison showing three types of events with different severity icons. Professional healthcare document aesthetic. Clean and educational.,A 45-second animated card with three distinct panels — Complaint light yellow, Grievance amber, Allegation red. Each shows the event type, definition, and required response action.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. The patient's son says: Last week someone left bruises on my father's arms during his bath. I want this reported officially. I'm calling the state. Is this a complaint, grievance, or allegation? What are your immediate steps, and what should you never say in this moment?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"When a patient or family files a formal grievance, a documented process begins. The agency has ten working days to respond in writing. That deadline is a CMS Conditions of Participation requirement — not a guideline. Your role as the field worker is intake and immediate escalation to your administrator or supervisor.",A professional home health supervisor reviewing a patient grievance document at a desk. Focused and organized. Clean office environment. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated timeline. Day 0: Grievance received. Day 10: Written response due. Arrow spans the ten-day window with action labels.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"The grievance process has six steps. One: receive the grievance — any staff member can receive it. Two: acknowledge and document everything — date, time, patient name, nature of concern. Three: submit to the administrator immediately — do not wait until the end of your shift. Four: the administrator investigates. Five: the patient receives a written response within ten working days. Six: the event is logged in the agency grievance register.",An administrator reviewing a written grievance resolution document with a patient-facing letter visible. Professional healthcare setting. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated six-step flowchart. Each step appears in sequence with a labeled icon. Step 3 highlights IMMEDIATELY in a different color. Step 5 shows a calendar with Day 10 circled.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. A patient calls your personal cell at seven PM. She says: I want to file a formal complaint about what happened today. The nurse was rude and I want it documented. You are not the administrator. What are your exact next steps? What do you document, and by when?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"When a patient or family is upset, the first sixty seconds of your response determine whether the situation stays manageable or escalates. Your goal is not to end the conversation. Your goal is to create the conditions for a professional one. That starts with listening and validating — not defending.",A calm and composed home health nurse standing in a doorway while a visibly upset family member gestures. The nurse's expression is focused and empathetic. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated scene. An escalating conversation bar graph flattens when the nurse uses active listening techniques. Text: The first 60 seconds matter.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M03 — Complaints & Grievances,Journey/M03/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"When a patient or family is upset, say: I hear your concern, and I want to make sure it is documented accurately. I am going to connect you with the right person right away. Then stop talking. Do not say: I didn't do anything wrong. Do not say: that's not what happened. Do not redirect them to your supervisor without first acknowledging their concern. Validate without admitting liability.",A nurse handing a business card to a family member with a calm and professional expression. Clean home entryway. Photorealistic. Dignified interaction.,A 45-second animation. Green speech bubble shows correct phrases. Red speech bubble shows forbidden phrases with an X. ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"Protected Health Information is any information that can identify a patient and relates to their health status, care, or payment. There are eighteen categories of PHI — name, address, date of birth, phone number, photos, and twelve others. A HIPAA violation does not require intent. Leaving a chart visible on your car seat is a violation. Discussing a patient by name in a public place is a violation.",A nurse closing a patient folder in her car with awareness of her surroundings. City setting visible through window. Photorealistic. Professional privacy awareness.,A 30-second animated card. Eighteen PHI category icons appear. Then bold text: Violation does not require intent. Two field scenario icons — chart on car seat and conversation in public — each with a red X.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"The minimum necessary standard means you use or disclose only the PHI needed to accomplish the specific task — nothing more. You are permitted to share PHI for three purposes without patient authorization: treatment with the direct care team, payment and billing, and healthcare operations such as quality review. You may not share PHI with an employer, with a family member who does not have authorization, or with anyone not directly involved in the patient's care.",A secure medical record icon surrounded by a shield with three labeled access zones: Treatment, Payment, Operations. Clean vector illustration style.,A 45-second animated card. Three green permission doors open — Treatment, Payment, Operations. Multiple red permission doors stay closed: employer family unauthorized third parties.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You are at your car outside a patient's building. A neighbor approaches and says: I've noticed you visiting Mrs. Johnson. Is she okay? We haven't seen her walking in weeks. The patient has signed no authorization for this person. What do you say?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"Every device you use for work is a HIPAA security asset. Your phone, your tablet, your work laptop, even the paperwork on your front seat. The field environment creates security risks that a clinical facility doesn't have — you work in patient homes, in your car, in public spaces. The Security Rule requires you to actively manage those risks every day.",A nurse locking her phone with a passcode before placing it in her bag. Her car is parked outside a patient's home. Clean and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Device icons appear — phone tablet laptop car. A security lock icon covers each one. Text: Every device is a HIPAA asset.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"Required: password or biometric lock on all work devices. Encrypted messaging only when sharing PHI. Use only agency-approved apps to access the EHR. Lock your car whenever patient documents are inside. Never photograph a patient without documented consent. Prohibited: texting PHI over personal SMS. Posting anything patient-related on social media. Accessing patient records over unsecured public Wi-Fi. Leaving printed records visible in a parked car.",A split panel image: left side shows secure practices with green indicators, right side shows prohibited behaviors with red X indicators. Clean and educational visual design.,A 45-second two-column animation. Left column: Required — each practice appears with a green checkmark. Right column: Prohibited — each behavior appears with a red X. Clean 2D style.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You are at your third visit when you realize you left a printed medication list at your second patient's home. The list includes name, date of birth, and full medication regimen. What are your obligations? What do you do right now?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"HIPAA gives patients four rights over their own information. The right to access their records. The right to amend inaccurate information. The right to an accounting of disclosures. And the right to request restrictions on use. When a breach may have occurred, your report to your Privacy Officer starts the breach notification process. The clock begins at discovery — not confirmation.",An elderly patient reviewing her own medical records with a nurse who is explaining the document. Professional and respectful interaction. Natural light. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Four patient rights icons appear in sequence. Then a clock animation: Discovery Day 0 — Notification deadline Day 60. Bold text: Report immediately.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"A breach is any unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of unsecured PHI that compromises its security or privacy. When you discover or suspect a breach, report to your Privacy Officer immediately — do not wait until your shift ends, do not wait for confirmation that harm occurred. The agency has sixty days to notify affected patients and Health and Human Services. Your immediate report is what starts that process.",A nurse on the phone reporting a concern to a supervisor with a serious and professional expression. Indoor setting. Natural light. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated breach response flowchart. Discovery icon — Immediate report to Privacy Officer — Agency investigation — 60-day notification deadline for HHS and affected patients.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M04 — HIPAA Privacy & Security,Journey/M04/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You sent a text with a patient's full name, diagnosis, medications, and visit notes. You realize you sent it to the wrong number. Is this a reportable breach? What are your next actions within the next thirty minutes?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"Standard precautions exist for one reason: you cannot tell who is infectious by looking at them. Many patients with bloodborne infections have no symptoms. A patient who looks and feels healthy can transmit HBV, HCV, or HIV through a single exposure. Standard precautions are not applied to high-risk patients — they are applied to all patients, all the time.",A home health nurse donning gloves before entering a patient's home. Clean, professional. Natural daylight. Photorealistic. Confident and safe demeanor.,A 30-second animated card. Patient silhouettes all labeled with a question mark. Standard precautions shield covers all of them equally. Text: Every patient. Every visit.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"Standard precautions apply to blood, all body fluids except sweat, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes. The five moments of hand hygiene are: before touching the patient, before any aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching the patient, and after touching patient surroundings. Soap and water for fifteen to twenty seconds. Alcohol-based hand rub for twenty to thirty seconds. Important: alcohol-based hand rub does not kill C. diff or norovirus. Use soap and water for those.",A nurse performing the five-moment hand hygiene process at a patient's kitchen sink. Step-by-step visual. Photorealistic. Clear and educational.,A 45-second animated five-moment sequence. Each moment appears with an icon and label. Timer shows 15-20 seconds for soap and water. Red alert icon for C. diff and norovirus: Use soap and water.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You arrive for wound care. No running water — the pipes froze. The wound dressing is saturated. Can you proceed? What is your decision process? What do you document?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"PPE selection must match the procedure's exposure risk. Wearing gloves for a blood draw is not enough if splatter is possible — you also need eye protection. Bag technique is your infection barrier between patients. If your bag touches a contaminated surface and then opens at your next patient's home, you have transferred that contamination.",A nurse opening her nursing bag on a disposable blue pad on a patient's kitchen table. Gloves on. Professional and deliberate. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. PPE icons match to procedure risk level. Bag technique diagram shows barrier placement on a surface.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"PPE matrix: gloves for any body fluid contact. Gown when fluid splash or environmental contamination is likely. Surgical mask for droplet precautions. N95 for airborne precautions. Eye protection for any splash risk during a procedure. Bag technique: place your bag on a disposable barrier — never on the floor, never on the kitchen counter without a barrier. Clean your hands before and after accessing the bag. Keep it closed when you are not actively retrieving supplies.",A nursing bag on a clean disposable barrier on a table next to a gloved nurse's hands. Professional infection control setup. Photorealistic.,A 45-second PPE matrix animation. Five procedure types each get the correct PPE icon highlighted. Then bag technique steps shown as clean numbered animation.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You enter the home for wound care. The patient's spouse and two children are visibly sick — coughing, sneezing, one child with a 103-degree fever. The patient is not symptomatic. What PPE do you select and why? Do you proceed? What do you document?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV is most effective when started within two hours of exposure. After seventy-two hours it loses its effectiveness entirely. Every minute between exposure and medical evaluation is part of the therapeutic window. The post-exposure response protocol is not a suggestion — it is a timed medical response.",A nurse washing her hands at a sink with urgency. Clock visible on the wall showing the current time. Photorealistic. Clean clinical feeling in a home setting.,A 30-second animated clock countdown card. HIV PEP effectiveness bar decreases after 2 hours and reaches zero at 72 hours. Bold text: Every minute counts.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"After a needlestick: one, remove your glove and wash the site with soap and water for at least thirty seconds. Two, call your supervisor immediately — not tomorrow, within two hours. Three, seek medical evaluation at the designated facility within two hours. This is where the PEP decision is made. Four, document source patient information to facilitate bloodborne pathogen testing if the patient consents. Five, complete the exposure incident report before you leave for the day.",A nurse at a sink washing her hands with soap and water with a focused expression. A phone is visible on the counter showing she will be calling next. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated 5-step protocol. Each step appears numbered with a time requirement label. Step 3 flashes with a 2-hour urgency indicator.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M05 — Infection Control,Journey/M05/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You are giving a subcutaneous injection. The needle slips and punctures your finger through your glove. The patient is known to have Hepatitis C. List your first four actions in the correct order. Include what you do with the patient, what you say, and your reporting timeline.",,, 
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"Communication barriers are not exceptions in home health. They are the rule. The average home health patient is elderly, managing multiple conditions, receiving complex medication instructions, and may have language, hearing, cognitive, or emotional barriers that affect every visit. Recognition is your first clinical skill.",A diverse elderly patient with a home health nurse. The nurse is leaning forward with active listening posture. A phone interpreter is on the table nearby. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated intro card. Patient silhouette surrounded by seven barrier icons. Text: Barriers are the rule — not the exception. Recognition is your first clinical skill.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"The seven categories are: Language — limited English proficiency or a different primary language. Physical — hearing loss, vision impairment, speech difficulties. Gender — care preferences or communication taboos related to gender. Cultural — different beliefs about illness, authority, or disclosure. Emotional — fear, grief, denial, or anxiety blocking the patient's ability to receive information. Perceptual — you and the patient interpret the same event differently. Interpersonal — distrust, past negative healthcare experiences, or power dynamics.",A clean infographic showing seven labeled barrier categories with a visual icon for each one. Medical illustration style on a white background.,A 45-second animated card. Seven numbered barrier icons appear one at a time with a one-sentence definition each. Clean and educational. Each icon uses a distinct color.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. Your patient speaks Tagalog with limited English. You need to explain a complex new insulin regimen. The patient's son offers to translate. Is this acceptable? What are the clinical risks of using a family member as an interpreter for clinical content? What is the correct action?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"A patient nodding does not mean a patient understood. Studies show patients forget forty to eighty percent of what clinicians tell them immediately after the encounter. The teach-back method is the only evidence-based technique that verifies actual comprehension — not just that information was delivered.",A nurse asking a patient to demonstrate how to use an insulin pen. The patient is attempting the demonstration. Focused and realistic interaction. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated split screen. Left: nurse talks — patient nods — question mark appears. Right: nurse asks patient to demonstrate — patient shows correct technique — green checkmark. Text: Teaching ≠ Learning.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"Teach-back in five steps. One: teach in small chunks — one concept at a time. Two: ask the patient to show you, not just confirm. Say: Can you show me how you will do this? Never ask: Do you understand? Three: if they can't demonstrate correctly, simplify, use visuals, and re-explain. Do not blame the patient. Four: repeat until the patient demonstrates correctly. Five: document the outcome.",A clean numbered list of five teach-back steps on a neutral background with a nurse icon demonstrating each step. Educational and professional.,A 45-second step-by-step animation. Five steps appear in sequence. Step 2 highlights the correct question versus the incorrect question in green and red. Step 5 shows documentation.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You taught insulin pen technique. During teach-back the patient dials 50 units instead of 5, then becomes embarrassed and says he's tired and wants to stop. What do you do now? What do you document? What is the specific safety concern if this patient self-administers tonight?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"Thirty-six percent of US adults have basic or below-basic health literacy. For your typical home health patient — elderly, managing multiple conditions, potentially speaking English as a second language — that rate is significantly higher. Your clinical instructions are competing with fear, pain, fatigue, and confusion. Plain language is not a courtesy. It is a clinical obligation.",A home health nurse sitting next to an elderly patient who is looking at a printed instruction sheet with obvious confusion. Warm indoor light. Empathetic interaction. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Stat callout: 36% of US adults have low health literacy. Then an icon of competing factors around a patient: fear pain fatigue confusion. Text: Plain language is clinical care.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"Plain language: write and speak at a fifth or sixth grade reading level. Give one instruction at a time. Use active language — say you should take this pill instead of the pill should be taken. Avoid medical jargon. Use visuals and demonstrations. For interpreter services: patients with limited English proficiency have a federal right under Title VI to a qualified interpreter at no cost. Family members may NOT interpret for informed consent, medication instructions, diagnosis, or clinical education.",A nurse holding up a simple illustrated patient instruction card while explaining to an elderly patient. Clear visual communication. Photorealistic. Warm home environment.,A 45-second animation. Plain language do's and don'ts appear. Then a Title VI interpreter rights banner. Family member icon with a red X over clinical content. Agency phone interpreter icon with a green checkmark.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M06 — Communication Barriers,Journey/M06/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. A patient asks you to review her care plan. She nods throughout. You notice she is holding the instruction sheet upside down, and she has not asked a single question. What does this observation tell you? What do you do next? What do you document?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"The Occupational Safety and Health Act covers you regardless of where you work. A patient's home is your workplace when you are in it. Your employer is required to assess workplace hazards including home environments, provide you with the PPE necessary to work safely, and cannot retaliate against you for raising a safety concern or refusing work that poses an imminent danger.",A home health nurse at the entrance of a patient's home surveying the environment before entering. Professional and alert expression. Suburban neighborhood setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. A home silhouette transforms into a workplace icon. Text: A patient's home is your workplace. OSH Act protections follow you inside.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"Your four OSHA rights are: the right to a safe workplace — your employer must identify and control hazards you encounter in the field. The right to information — you can request a Safety Data Sheet for any chemical you are exposed to. The right to refuse imminently dangerous work — a serious and immediate threat entitles you to refuse without fear of retaliation. And the right to file a confidential complaint with OSHA at 1-800-321-OSHA.",Four shield icons labeled with OSHA rights on a clean white background. Professional safety communication style.,A 45-second animated card. Four OSHA right shields appear in sequence. Shield 3 highlights: Refuse Imminent Danger — No Retaliation. Shield 4 shows the OSHA phone number.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. You arrive and smell a strong chemical odor. The family says they mixed bleach and ammonia to clean. Your eyes are burning. The patient is in the bedroom. What hazard is present? What is the immediate risk to you and the patient? What are your first actions?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"The Globally Harmonized System standardizes how chemical hazards are communicated on labels and Safety Data Sheets. Nine hazard pictograms identify the type of hazard at a glance — flammable, corrosive, toxic. A Safety Data Sheet has sixteen sections. Section eight is the one you use most — it tells you exactly what PPE is required and what the exposure limits are.",A GHS chemical label graphic with nine pictogram icons clearly visible. Professional chemical safety design. Clean educational illustration.,A 30-second animated SDS explainer. Nine GHS pictogram icons appear labeled. SDS document opens to Section 8 highlighted in orange. Text: Section 8 = Your PPE requirements.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"A GHS label has six required elements: product identifier, signal word — danger or warning, hazard statements, precautionary statements, pictograms, and supplier information. In the field, Section 8 of the SDS is your practical reference — it tells you the glove type, respiratory protection level, and eye protection required. If you find an unlabeled container or an unfamiliar chemical in a patient's home, do not use it. Request an SDS or contact poison control at 1-800-222-1222.",A nurse examining an unlabeled spray bottle with a cautious expression before setting it aside and reaching for her phone. Realistic home setting. Photorealistic.,A 45-second animated GHS label breakdown. Six label elements appear labeled. Then a field scenario: unlabeled container — nurse sets it aside — calls poison control. Text: When in doubt don't use it.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. A patient hands you an unlabeled spray bottle. She says the doctor used it to clean around the wound last time. The bottle has a faint chemical smell. You don't recognize it. What do you do? What risks are you protecting against? What do you tell the patient?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"Incident reporting is not a punitive process. It is the safety system. A near-miss report — something that almost caused harm but didn't — is equally as important as an injury report, because near misses reveal systemic hazards before they injure someone. Your report protects the next employee who faces the same situation.",A nurse submitting an incident report on a tablet with a focused professional expression. Clean office environment visible in the background. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Two icons: Injury report and Near-Miss report — both shown as equally important inputs to a safety system. Text: Your report protects the next worker.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"Workplace injury: notify your supervisor immediately — do not wait until the end of your shift. Complete the incident report within twenty-four hours. Seek medical evaluation if the injury requires treatment. Your report triggers the OSHA three-hundred log entry. For medical device reporting: if a device malfunction causes or could cause patient death or serious injury, report to your supervisor immediately. The administrator has ten working days to submit FDA Form 3500A. Do not return or repair the device until risk management clears it.",A flowchart graphic showing workplace injury reporting steps and FDA MDR reporting steps as two parallel pathways. Professional and clean design.,A 45-second two-pathway animation. Left: Workplace injury — Immediate supervisor notification — 24-hour report — OSHA 300 log. Right: Device malfunction — Supervisor — 10 working days — FDA Form 3500A.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M07 — Workplace & Patient Safety (OSHA),Journey/M07/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. During a transfer assist, the hospital bed rail collapses. The patient falls and has a hip bruise. She refuses to go to the hospital. List your first three immediate actions. What do you document about the device? Is this an MDR-reportable event and why?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"The Patient Bill of Rights is not a mission statement. It is a legally enforceable set of protections under the CMS Conditions of Participation at 42 CFR 484.50. Every patient receives these rights at admission and must be reminded of them on request. You are personally responsible for upholding them at every visit.",A nurse handing a Patient Bill of Rights document to an elderly patient at his kitchen table. Professional and respectful. Warm home setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Patient Bill of Rights document icon with a shield labeled 42 CFR 484.50. Text: Legally enforceable. Not optional. You are responsible.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"Seven core rights in home health. The right to be informed — in their language about their care and diagnosis. The right to participate in care planning, including the right to refuse treatment. The right to privacy and confidentiality. The right to dignity and respect regardless of their condition or behavior. The right to receive care without discrimination. The right to voice grievances without retaliation. And the right to be informed of charges before care begins. Every visit is an opportunity to either uphold or violate these rights.",A clean numbered list infographic showing seven patient rights with a brief label for each. Professional healthcare design.,A 45-second animated card. Seven rights appear sequentially numbered. Each right has a brief scenario icon showing what upholding it looks like in a home health visit.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. The patient says she doesn't want wound care today — she's tired and has visitors coming. At your last visit three days ago, the wound showed early signs of infection. What patient right is at stake? What are your clinical and documentation obligations? Can you proceed without consent?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"An advance directive is the patient's legally recognized voice for a time when they can no longer speak for themselves. Honoring it — even when a family member is pressuring you not to — is both an ethical obligation and a legal requirement. The patient made this decision when they had capacity. Your role is to honor it.",A DNR document on a refrigerator door in a patient's home. Clear and visible. A nurse is noting its location on her tablet. Photorealistic. Clean and sobering.,A 30-second animated card. An advance directive document appears. Family pressure icon with an X. Shield labeled Patient's Voice with a green checkmark. Text: The document controls.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"Know your advance directive types. A DNR means do not attempt CPR — it must be physician-signed and on file. A POLST is more comprehensive and covers intubation, hospitalization, and artificial nutrition decisions. A Living Will contains the patient's specific instructions for end-of-life care. A Healthcare Power of Attorney designates who makes decisions if the patient loses capacity. Your obligations are clear: know whether a directive exists, document its location in every visit note, and never attempt resuscitation if a valid DNR is on file.",Four labeled directive document icons side by side: DNR, POLST, Living Will, Healthcare POA. Clean medical illustration.,A 45-second animated card. Four directive types defined sequentially. Three field obligations appear at the end: Know it — Document its location — Honor it.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. The patient is unresponsive with agonal breathing. A valid physician-signed DNR is on the refrigerator. Her son grabs your arm and says: ignore that paper, save her, she changed her mind. What is the legally and clinically correct response? What do you do and document?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"As a home health worker, you are a mandatory reporter under California law. You are legally required to report suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of elderly or dependent adults. The threshold is reasonable suspicion — not proof. You do not investigate. You report. Failure to report when you had reasonable suspicion is a misdemeanor.",A focused home health nurse documenting observations on a tablet after noticing concerning signs on a patient. Serious and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Mandatory reporter badge icon. Threshold meter showing: Proof not required — Suspicion is sufficient. Bold text: Report. Don't investigate.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"Physical abuse indicators: unexplained bruising, especially bilateral bruising at the same stage of healing, fractures, burns, and grip marks. Emotional abuse: fearfulness, withdrawal, or visible anxiety when the caregiver is present. Sexual abuse: bruising or injury to genital areas, or patient disclosure. Financial abuse: sudden changes in assets, unpaid bills when resources should be available, a caregiver controlling access to money. Neglect: dehydration, malnutrition, untreated wounds, unsanitary conditions beyond the patient's ability to control. Document what you observe — objectively, factually, and immediately.",A clinical illustration showing observable abuse indicators grouped by type. Medical education style. Neutral and factual. No graphic violence.,A 45-second animated categorized list. Each abuse type appears with observable indicators and brief documentation guidance. Clean and educational tone.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M08 — Patient Rights & Responsibilities,Journey/M08/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. The patient has bilateral bruises at different stages of healing. She says she bumps into things. Her adult grandson, the primary caregiver, is in the room. She looks at the floor when he speaks and avoids eye contact. List your observations, your suspicion level, and your exact reporting obligations and timeline.",,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"A corporate compliance program exists to prevent, detect, and correct violations before they become legal events. Without a compliance program, a single billing error can become a False Claims Act case. A single undisclosed payment can become an Anti-Kickback violation. Every employee is part of the program — including you.",A professional healthcare compliance meeting with a diverse staff group reviewing documents. Conference room setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Three pillars labeled: Prevent — Detect — Correct. Each shows a relevant scenario icon. Text: Every employee is part of the program.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"The seven OIG elements are: written policies and standards of conduct, a designated Compliance Officer, effective training and education for all employees, open lines of communication including anonymous reporting, internal monitoring and auditing, consistent enforcement and discipline, and prompt corrective action. Your personal role in this program is simple: complete required training, report concerns promptly through authorized channels, and never falsify documentation.",A clean pyramid infographic showing the 7 OIG compliance program elements. Professional corporate compliance design. Clean and educational.,A 45-second animated pyramid build. Seven elements appear from bottom to top. Your role appears at the bottom of the screen: Complete Training — Report Concerns — Never Falsify.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 1/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. Your supervisor says: just sign the visit note for last Thursday. We know you were there. The EVV system didn't record it. I need it submitted today for billing. You were at the visit. What is the compliance issue? What do you do?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 1 — Summary,"Every visit note you complete feeds into a Medicare or Medicaid claim. Every claim is a federal attestation that the care was medically necessary and properly delivered. Rounding up your visit time. Documenting a service you didn't provide. Signing a note without reviewing it. These are not administrative errors — they are potential False Claims Act violations.",A nurse completing a visit note on a tablet with a Medicare claim document visible overlaid in a transparent layer. Symbolic and professional. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Visit note transforms into a Medicare claim. Bold text: Your documentation = a federal attestation. FCA consequence icons appear.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 2 — Content,"The False Claims Act imposes civil penalties of thirteen thousand to twenty-six thousand dollars per false claim, plus treble damages. Criminal penalties include up to five years in prison. The Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits anything of value exchanged to induce referrals — this includes gift cards, meals, and favors between employees and vendors. Remember the 60-day rule: if the agency identifies an overpayment from Medicare or Medicaid, it must be returned within sixty days of identification. Keeping an identified overpayment is itself a false claim.",A legal scales icon with FCA dollar amounts on one side and compliance checkmark on the other. Professional legal compliance design.,A 45-second animated card. FCA penalties displayed. AKS examples appear: gift card meal favor — each with a red X. 60-day clock animation for overpayment return.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 2/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. Your coworker says she always adds five to seven minutes to her EVV entries. She says the company bills more and everyone does it. Is this fraud, waste, or abuse? What is your obligation? What is the personal risk to your coworker and the risk to the agency?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 1 — Summary,"Multiple federal laws protect employees who report compliance concerns in good faith. The False Claims Act, HIPAA, and OSHA all contain anti-retaliation provisions. You cannot be terminated, demoted, harassed, or have your hours reduced because you made a report. The compliance hotline exists specifically for this purpose.",A nurse confidently picking up a phone to call a compliance hotline. Professional and empowered expression. Clean office setting. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Three federal law shields: FCA, HIPAA, OSHA. Each shows anti-retaliation icon. Text: You are protected. Report without fear.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 2 — Content,"Three internal reporting channels: your direct supervisor for general concerns, the Compliance Officer for compliance-specific issues, and the anonymous hotline for any concern where you want confidentiality. External channel: the OIG Hotline at 1-800-HHS-TIPS for fraud involving federal programs. The False Claims Act also contains a qui tam provision — if you bring a lawsuit about fraud against the federal government and it is validated, you may receive fifteen to thirty percent of the government's recovery.",A clean reporting flowchart showing three internal channels and one external channel with labeled icons. Professional compliance communications design.,A 45-second animated reporting channel map. Three internal pathways to a compliance officer icon. External pathway to OIG hotline. Qui tam callout with percentage icon for financial protection.,45 seconds
ACHC-ART-M09 — Corporate Compliance,Journey/M09/Lesson 3/Card 3 — Challenge,"Scenario. Three weeks ago you reported a billing concern through the anonymous hotline. This week your hours were cut thirty percent and you received your first negative performance review in two years. Nothing else changed. Do you have a retaliation claim? What is your evidence? What are your options?",,, 
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 1/Card 1 — Summary,"Healthcare ethics governs decisions where law and policy are silent, ambiguous, or in conflict with each other. The four bioethical principles — autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice — provide a framework for the hardest decisions you will face in the field. Learning to apply them before you encounter the situation is what makes the difference.",A home health nurse pausing thoughtfully before entering a patient's room. Contemplative and professional. Warm corridor light. Photorealistic.,A 30-second animated card. Four principle icons appear: Autonomy — Beneficence — Non-maleficence — Justice. Text: Ethics applies where policy is silent.,30 seconds
ACHC-ART-M10 — Ethics in Healthcare,Journey/M10/Lesson 1/Card 2 — Content,"The four principles are: Autonomy — the patient's right to make decisions about their own care, even ones you disagree with. Beneficence — your duty to act in the patient's best interest. Non-maleficence — your duty to avoid causing harm, including harm from inaction. And Justice — fair, equitable access to care regardless of race, religion, ability to pay, or social status. When principles conflict — most commonly when patient autonomy and non-maleficence are in tension — the Ethics Committee is available for consultation.",Four labeled principle definition cards in a clean grid. Medical ethics education visual style. Professional and neutral.,A 45-second animated card. Four principles defined one at a time with a healthcare home visit scenario for each. Ethics Committee consultation icon appears at the end for conflict resolution.,45 seconds
